Axolotl
Ambystoma mexicanum

The axolotl is a mole salamander of Mexico’s highland wetlands, with its surviving natural habitat concentrated around Xochimilco. Rather than metamorphosing into a land-dwelling salamander, it reaches reproductive maturity while retaining larval features such as external gills and a finned tail. Its remarkable limb and tissue regeneration makes it a major developmental model, but laboratory findings do not promise human treatments. After a limb is amputated, a specialized wound epidermis covers the stump, where cells gather into a blastema, a growth zone that rebuilds missing structures; experiments show that nerve signals are needed for its growth.

Adults average about 20 centimetres, and some exceed 30; age, sex and rearing conditions influence size. Wild-type animals are dark brown, olive or blackish with mottling; captive lines also include pink-bodied leucistic and pale-eyed albino forms. Three pairs of feathery external gills project from the head, above a long tail edged by a low fin. Four short limbs have slender digits. Gills and vascularized skin absorb dissolved oxygen from water, while simple lungs let the axolotl breathe air at the surface. Mature males tend to have a swollen cloaca, while egg-bearing females may have a fuller abdomen.

Historically, axolotls inhabited freshwater lakes and wetlands across the Mexican Central Valley, including Xochimilco and Chalco; Lake Chalco was later drained. The canal network of Xochimilco, south of Mexico City, is the best-documented modern natural habitat; the 2019 IUCN assessment also listed records from other sites. These cool, high-altitude waters have muddy bottoms, aquatic plants and channels woven through cultivated chinampas. Chinampa refuge canals combine habitat structure with local farming and wetland restoration.

Young larvae eat zooplankton, including small crustaceans, and laboratory trials show that prey choice changes as they grow. Larger axolotls are carnivores; wild gut samples and food-web studies find varied aquatic invertebrate and fish prey, though adult field data remain limited. The axolotl approaches prey closely, then rapidly opens its mouth and lowers the floor of its mouth, drawing water and prey inward by suction. Laboratory tests with Xochimilco water found that contamination reduced feeding by axolotl larvae.

Axolotls swim through waves of bending that pass along the body and tail, a motion documented in adults. Their external gills remain functional in adulthood, and their vascularized skin also exchanges gases with water. Courtship is the clearest documented adult social interaction: a male nudges a female and leads her to a sperm packet on the bottom. Studies have detected male proteins released into the water during courtship, evidence for chemical communication.

During courtship, the male deposits a spermatophore that the female takes up with her cloaca, enabling internal fertilization. In controlled UAM Xochimilco breeding, females laid roughly 300–600 eggs, attaching them to plants or other submerged surfaces. Transparent egg coverings reveal development; one university study recorded hatching about 15 days after laying under laboratory conditions. Newly hatched larvae feed on small zooplankton, with intake changing as they grow. Their limbs develop progressively while adults retain the larval body plan and external gills. Laboratory studies place female maturity around 12–18 months; growth varies with rearing conditions, and comparable wild-age data are scarce.

As a predator, the axolotl links zooplankton and other small aquatic animals to larger consumers in the Xochimilco food web. Introduced carp and tilapia eat some of the same prey as axolotls, and carp stomach samples have also contained axolotl eggs. Vegetated chinampa edges and filtered refuge canals can shelter axolotls from invasive fish and improve local water conditions. A release study documented survival and foraging at two sites, but also recorded a great egret capturing an axolotl in Xochimilco; releases alone cannot prove population recovery.

The IUCN SSC Amphibian Specialist Group assessed the axolotl as Critically Endangered globally on 23 October 2019; the assessment appeared in the 2020 Red List. The assessment estimated an observed decline of more than 80 percent over three generations (16.5 years), associated with urban habitat change, water pollution and introduced fish. Drainage and conversion erased much of the historic lake habitat, while remaining canals face urban pressure and degraded water quality. This wild crisis is distinct from extensive captive and research colonies; laboratory abundance does not mean Xochimilco has recovered. UNAM researchers and chinamperos have built filtered refuge canals that pair habitat restoration with local agriculture.

Bactrian camel
Camelus bactrianus

The two-humped Bactrian camel is a domestic livestock species of Central and East Asia, valued for transport, milk, meat and fibre. Its scientific name is Camelus bactrianus; the distinct wild camel is Camelus ferus.

Two separated humps distinguish it from the dromedary. Domestic Bactrians are sturdy, shaggy-haired camels, often dark to sandy brown; males tend to be larger. Humps store fat, not water, and the thick winter coat is shed in warmer weather.

Domestic herds occur across Inner, Central and East Asia, notably Mongolia and China. Herders keep them in steppe, semi-desert and desert environments, moving with seasonal forage and temperature; these managed ranges are not a single wild habitat.

It grazes grasses and browses dry, salty or thorny plants. A split upper lip helps it take coarse forage; it regurgitates and rechews food. In snowy winters, Bactrians dig through snow for plants. Hump fat supplies energy when feed is scarce.

Social groups commonly include females, young and a dominant male; excluded males may form bachelor groups. Males display or fight for mates. Calls and scent aid communication. Herders guide managed groups between pastures and use camels for riding or carrying loads.
Spring mating is commonly reported. After about 12–14 months’ gestation, females usually bear one calf; twins are rare. Newborns walk within a day and nurse for roughly one to two years.

Domestic camels convert sparse steppe and desert vegetation into transport, milk, meat and fibre for herding households. Their grazing occurs within managed systems; effects on plants depend on local herd density, mobility and pasture conditions.

Critical-endangerment listings for the “wild Bactrian camel” concern Camelus ferus, not this domestic species. Camelus bactrianus remains livestock; a wildlife extinction-risk category is not a measure of the condition of its domestic herds. Conditions and pressures affecting domestic herds require region-specific assessment.

Baikal seal
Pusa sibirica

The Baikal seal, or nerpa, is a true seal whose entire natural range lies in Lake Baikal, southern Siberia. It is the only mammal native to the lake and the only seal species living exclusively in freshwater.

Adults are about 1.1–1.4 metres long; males are slightly larger at physical maturity. The FAO guide reports adults around 80–90 kilograms. Like other true seals, the Baikal seal has no visible external ear flaps; its foreflippers steer while its hind flippers propel it underwater.
This freshwater seal is endemic to Lake Baikal and its connecting streams. In winter, seals breathe through holes in the ice, while females shelter newborns in snow lairs on the frozen lake.

Baikal seals hunt underwater, taking small endemic golomyanka and sculpins as well as other freshwater fishes; the mix changes with season and location. They also eat amphipods, tiny crustaceans that form dense swarms in some parts of the lake. Video and tag data show seals pursuing these prey at night, when amphipods rise in the water column and fish shift into shallower depths. Behind the canines, its cheek teeth have closely spaced cusps that form a comb-like filter. This lets it expel water while retaining tiny prey, making repeated captures more efficient.

Most seals forage alone and remain spread across the lake in winter, although several may share access to an ice hole. Instrumented seals commonly dived for 10–20 minutes to depths of 50–200 metres; the greatest depth reported in the FAO guide was 300 metres. Baikal seals have been heard vocalizing both above and below water, and reported sound types differ between sexes; recordings remain scarce, so their social function is not settled.

Pups are born in snow lairs on lake ice from mid-February through March. Newborns measure about 64–66 centimetres, weigh 4–4.2 kilograms and have white lanugo, a soft first coat. They stay in the den and generally avoid water for their first two or three weeks. Mating takes place in water, mainly in the first half of April, and pregnancy lasts about 11 months. Lactation lasts around 2.5 months and overlaps with the mating season.

By eating amphipods directly, it draws energy from a lower level of the food chain than when it eats fish that consume those crustaceans. This shorter pathway loses less energy between successive consumers and helps explain how a nutrient-poor lake supports many seals.

Goodman’s IUCN assessment lists Least Concern; it was assessed on 10 July 2015 and published in 2016. Commercial hunting rose in the twentieth century; the population grew after early-century hunting but later declined with harvest and distemper outbreaks. A distemper-related morbillivirus epidemic struck the population in 1987–1988. Pollution, bycatch, illegal hunting and shrinking breeding ice remain concerns. A 2022 field project reported that tourist activity can disturb seals at the Ushkanyi Islands haul-outs.

Banded mongoose
Mungos mungo
The banded mongoose is a small, day-active African carnivore whose dark transverse back bands distinguish it from other mongooses. It lives in mixed social groups that rear their litters communally.

Adults measure about 30–45 cm from head to rump, with a tail of 15–30 cm and a reported mass of 1.5–2.5 kg. The coarse coat ranges from pale to reddish brown, with dark bars starting midway along the back, dark feet and a black tail tip. Each forefoot bears five clawed digits and each hind foot four; rear claws are shorter and blunter, while rounded cheek teeth help crush hard prey.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, banded mongooses occupy forest, savanna, shrubland and grassland. Field studies recorded dens in termite mounds, erosion gullies, aardvark holes and sometimes human structures; most were used briefly, though a few favored dens were reused for weeks.

In a two-year Ugandan study, beetles and millipedes dominated food records, while vertebrate remains occurred in only 12% of droppings. Other observations include termites, grasshoppers, worms, fruit, reptiles, small mammals, birds and eggs; to crack an egg or a snail’s shell, a mongoose may throw it backward between its hind legs against a stone or other hard surface.

A Ugandan field study reported packs of six to 35 adults and subadults; group size varies, and individuals forage for prey while the pack travels together. Frequent close calls help maintain group contact during foraging, when animals often work with their heads lowered to dig. Experimental work found that recruitment calls convey urgency or risk rather than a fixed label for each stimulus. In the Ugandan study population, younger males tended to provide more babysitting than older males, so care is not divided equally among group members.

Females can breed from about one year old and, in the long-studied Ugandan population, several females often give birth together, sometimes on the same day; females there may breed repeatedly through the year. Gestation lasts close to two months, and typical litters contain two to six blind, sparsely furred pups; eyes begin opening at about ten days. Pups leave the den at three to four weeks, then usually form a close escort relationship with an adult that feeds, carries, grooms and protects them until nutritional independence at roughly three months; care received predicts survival to nutritional independence and greater mass at one year in that study population.

In the studied Ugandan population, competition for food and mates across the population increased the probability of encounters between groups. Conflicts were also associated with periods of group growth and with reduced litter and adult survival.

The global IUCN assessment completed on 28 February 2015 and published in 2016 listed the species as Least Concern, citing its broad range, common occurrence, protected-area presence and tolerance of human-modified places; that assessment reported a stable trend. A serious regional exception is documented in northern Botswana: the mongoose-associated bacterium Mycobacterium mungi caused repeated outbreaks and high mortality in troops living near people during 2000–2010. The study did not establish the pathogen’s full host range or transmission to humans, and this local disease record should not be generalized to the species across Africa.

Barn swallow
Hirundo rustica

The Barn Swallow is a small, agile passerine that breeds across much of the Northern Hemisphere and moves south when cold weather reduces flying-insect food. Many European populations cross to Africa for winter. Most North American breeders winter in Central or South America. A small breeding population is established in Argentina, well south of the main Northern Hemisphere range. Its use of barns and other buildings brings it close to people, but it remains a wild aerial hunter.

Adults are about 15–18 cm long and weigh roughly 17–20 g; pointed wings and long outer tail feathers give them a swift, deeply forked silhouette. Plumage varies across geographic forms: European birds are relatively pale below, while North American birds are generally darker underneath. Males usually have longer tail streamers than females.

For breeding, the species needs open airspace rich in flying insects, including meadows, grazed fields, shorelines and wetlands. It commonly attaches a nest to a sheltered beam or ledge in a barn, shed or other outbuilding. Wet mud nearby supplies building material, and shelter helps protect the nest.

Barn Swallows are aerial insectivores: they catch flies, beetles, bees, wasps, ants and moths in flight, often low over grass or water, turning quickly to seize prey. They often select larger individual insects; swallowed grit or tiny shell fragments may help grind food or supply calcium. A farm study linked livestock presence with more large fly and beetle prey in the swallow’s diet.

The swallow’s agile flight lets it skim over water to drink or bathe without landing. Pairs nest alone or in loose colonies, and migrants gather in communal roosts. Its twittering song and short calls help maintain contact.

The pair builds a cup of mud pellets, often mixed with grass and lined with feathers, on a sheltered wall or beam. A typical clutch contains four or five eggs. In Britain, the female usually incubates them for 16–18 days, with occasional help from the male. Chicks hatch altricial, meaning helpless and sparsely feathered, and both parents feed them insects. In Ontario, young fledge at about 19–24 days; parents may continue feeding them for up to a week after they leave the nest.

By feeding on flying insects, the swallow is both predator and prey: diurnal raptors hunt adults, while rats and squirrels may raid nests in Canada. House Sparrows compete for nest sites and can destroy eggs or chicks; nest parasites can also reduce breeding success.

Trends vary by region. Canada’s 2021 COSEWIC assessment classed the species as Special Concern, after a Threatened assessment in 2011; national numbers were broadly stable from 2009 to 2019 following a longer decline. Declining insect prey, severe spring temperature swings, agricultural change and some nest-site losses remain concerns, though causes are not fully understood. In the UK, BTO records a 23% breeding-population fall from 1995 to 2024; it also identifies agricultural intensification and winter survival as possible influences.

Barnacle Goose
Branta leucopsis

The Barnacle Goose is a compact, strongly social Arctic goose whose annual life follows a long migration between northern breeding grounds and milder European wintering areas. Three principal flyway populations breed in northeast Greenland, Svalbard and the Russian Arctic, including Baltic regions; their winter destinations differ, so conservation counts track them separately.

Adults have a black head, neck and breast, sharply set off by a complete creamy-white face; the upper body is blue-grey with fine black bars, while the belly is pale. The short black bill and legs, white tail patch and compact body complete a distinctive pattern. At 58–70 cm long, with a wingspan around 132–145 cm, it is a relatively small goose. Canada Goose is larger and has a black neck with a white chinstrap, not the Barnacle Goose’s full white face.

Arctic breeders use tundra coasts, offshore islets and, in some colonies, ledges on steep cliffs; nesting on islands or heights can reduce access by terrestrial predators. After hatching, families move to tundra, coastal marshes and freshwater margins. During migration and winter, flocks use estuaries, tidal flats, saltmarshes and open grassland, and often graze on agricultural pasture. In northwestern Europe, some descendants of established or escaped birds also breed on temperate islands and lakes.

This is a grazing herbivore: its stubby bill clips grass leaves and shoots close to the ground, and it also takes sedges, mosses, buds and other tundra plants as availability changes. Goslings pick vegetation for themselves soon after hatching rather than being fed by their parents. Like other grazing geese, it processes abundant, fibrous forage rapidly; frequent feeding and cropping young growth help meet the high energy costs of migration and egg production.

Barnacle Geese remain vocal and sociable, gathering into large flocks outside the breeding season and travelling in noisy lines or V-shaped formations. Pairs maintain close bonds, and parents accompany and defend their young within family groups. Their repeated barking calls help keep flock members in contact, especially in flight and at crowded roosts. Seasonal movements connect northern breeding areas with wintering sites in Britain, Ireland, the Netherlands and adjacent coasts.

Pairs nest once each year, usually in a colony. Depending on the population and local predators, a nest may sit on a cliff ledge, a small island or low ground; cliff nesting is not universal. The female usually incubates four to five eggs for about 24–25 days while her mate guards nearby. Downy, precocial goslings leave the nest soon after hatching and feed themselves; both parents guide and protect them. Only cliff-nesting colonies require the famous descent: chicks follow adults down to feeding areas, sometimes by leaping from ledges. They can fly at about 40–45 days and remain with family through their first winter.

On Svalbard, the availability of nutritious plants affects nesting success: females feeding on poorer vegetation spend longer away from their nests, increasing exposure of eggs to predators. Droppings return nutrients to feeding and roosting sites, while seeds may be moved between patches. Eggs and young are vulnerable to Arctic foxes, polar bears, and adults can be taken by raptors. On temperate wintering grounds, concentrated grazing sometimes brings geese into conflict with farmers.

The Barnacle Goose is globally listed as Least Concern in BTO’s species account. AEWA’s 2024 report estimated about 1.4 million birds in the Russia–Netherlands/Germany flyway population in January 2023, following decades of growth and signs of recent stabilization. Protection of breeding and wintering wetlands, coordinated counts and management of crop damage remain important. Arctic habitat change, hunting and disturbance require attention alongside the benefits and pressures created by expanding populations.

Beech marten
Martes foina

The beech marten is a medium-sized mustelid with a long, supple body, short legs and a bushy tail. Its native range spans much of Europe and central Asia east to the Himalaya and north-west China. It uses woodland, rocky slopes and settled landscapes, and in parts of Europe regularly shelters in buildings. The species is also called the stone marten. An introduced population has been reported in southeastern Wisconsin, outside its native range; this isolated record should not be confused with the native American marten, a different species.

Adults generally have sandy to dark brown fur, a cream-white throat and chest patch, rounded ears and a long tail; the head is elongated and angular. The pale bib often forks and may extend down the forelegs. The fur on the underside of the paws is sparse, a useful close-view distinction from the Eurasian pine marten. That relative, Martes martes, usually has a smaller yellowish or cream bib, larger ears and furrier feet. The beech marten’s pinkish-brown nose contrasts with the darker nose of Martes martes. Adults typically measure 45–60 cm head–body, with a 25–30 cm tail, and weigh 1.2–2.3 kg.

Across its range the species occupies deciduous woodland, scrub, forest edges, open rocky ground and farmland. In southern Portugal, radio-tracked martens used structurally complex cork-oak woodland together with riparian strips, orchards and pasture; foraging and resting sites differed by sex and landscape scale. In several central European regions, animals also occupy villages and cities, nesting in attics, barns, garages or wall cavities. Urban tolerance is not universal: the IUCN account reports greater woodland association in Israel. Habitat use therefore reflects local resources and landscape, rather than a simple preference for either forest or people.

The beech marten is an opportunistic omnivore. It takes small mammals, birds and eggs, reptiles, invertebrates and carrion, as well as fruit and other plant material. Stomach analyses in central Greece found animal prey especially prominent in spring, when small vertebrates and arthropods were frequent; fruits and insects became more important in summer and autumn as seasonal foods ripened. The pattern shifted among seasons and individuals, rather than following one fixed menu.

Beech martens forage mainly at night and spend daylight hours in sheltered resting places. They are generally solitary outside breeding; scent marks signal territorial boundaries. In two towns in Luxembourg, radio-tracked animals held stable territories through the year, mostly within the urban boundary; territories of males and females overlapped little with those of the same sex. Urban living did not erase this spacing pattern. Local food and shelter can bring individuals into human structures, while their routine movements still follow territorial boundaries.

Mating occurs in summer, but birth follows the next spring because development pauses after fertilization. A study of more than 100 animals from the Bordeaux region documented about eight months of delayed implantation, ending in late February; implantation is followed by roughly 30 days of active gestation. Litters are born around late March or early April. The young are initially helpless and remain in a den while the mother nurses them. In the Bordeaux study, nursing could continue until mid-May. After weaning, juveniles continue to develop and learn to forage before becoming independent later in the year. The long pause separates mating from the brief period of embryo growth and birth.

In Bussaco National Forest in central Portugal, a study recovered seeds from stone-marten scats and tested their germination, including seeds of native plants and introduced cherry laurel. Gut passage increased and accelerated germination of native elmleaf blackberry, Rubus ulmifolius, but did not measurably affect cherry laurel; preference for that introduced fruit may nonetheless help it spread. Martens also used orchards, woodland edges and buildings in the southern Portuguese landscape studied by radio-tracking, linking their ecology to cultivated and less-modified patches.

Published in 2016 from an assessment dated 3 March 2015, the IUCN classified the species as Least Concern globally, citing its broad range, large population and occurrence in protected areas. Persecution and fur hunting occur locally, but assessors found no evidence of widespread decline from these pressures. Jordan’s 2020 national mammal Red Data Book lists the species as Endangered there and cites habitat degradation and direct killing, illustrating how regional circumstances differ.

American bison
Bison bison

The American bison is a large hoofed ruminant native to North America. Before European settlement, it ranged from northern Mexico to interior Alaska. Two forms are commonly distinguished: plains bison in the south and wood bison farther north.

Its massive head, shoulder hump and short hindquarters create a distinctive profile. Both sexes have short, curved horns. Long hair covers the head, shoulders and forelegs, but the rear coat is shorter. Adults shed much of this winter coat in spring. Plains bison usually have a smaller, rounder hump than wood bison.

Bison use grasslands, prairies, sedge meadows, shrublands and some woods. Historically, herds moved over immense areas. Today, free-ranging and conservation herds occupy fragments of the former range; fences and management often limit movement.
Bison graze year-round, mainly on grasses and sedges, as well as flowering plants and leaves when available. In winter, they sweep snow aside with the head to uncover plants. They need water daily.

Herds vary with sex, age and season: females and young commonly group together, while mature bulls may be solitary or form male groups. Bison alternate grazing, resting and rumination. They move as food and water change, wallow in loose soil, and bulls clash during the summer rut.

Mating occurs mainly from late June to September. After about 285 days, a female usually gives birth to one calf in spring. The reddish calf soon follows the herd, nurses for seven to eight months and is weaned by its first year. Females may breed at two to three years; males often breed later.

Grazing, trampling, wallowing and movement disturb prairie plants and soils, creating varied growing conditions. Seeds caught in the coat travel elsewhere, while dung returns nutrients to soil. These effects create a mosaic of plant communities and small habitats, shaped by landscape and herd management.

The global IUCN Red List assessment, dated 1 September 2016 and published in 2017, classified the species as Near Threatened. It counted wild and conservation herds, not commercial livestock; most American bison are managed for production. The assessment cited few viable populations and many small, isolated herds. It also identified habitat loss and genetic risks, including cattle introgression and hybridization between subspecies.

European bison
Bison bonasus

The European bison, or wisent, is Europe’s largest land mammal. Hunting and habitat loss erased its free-living populations; descendants of a small managed breeding group later founded reintroduced herds.

Adult bulls are larger than cows and have more muscular forequarters, a shoulder hump, and thicker, wider-set horns. Both sexes have short horns, a long-haired head and forebody with a beard, and shorter rear hair; the coat ranges from tawny to dark brown. At Białowieża, adult bulls weigh 440–920 kg and can reach 188 cm at the withers; cows weigh 320–640 kg. Their forequarters are less developed and their horns curve more inward.

Wisent use woodland mosaics with meadows and clearings, as well as forest-steppe and mountain forest–meadow landscapes. In Białowieża, records include mixed woods, alder stands and river meadows. Closed forest alone may limit winter forage, prompting movements into farmland. Historical records also place them in forest-steppe, so they are not strict forest specialists. Reintroduced free-ranging herds were established from 1952.

They ruminate and eat grasses, sedges, herbs and woody plants. DNA metabarcoding in Białowieża found 105 plant taxa during the growing season; woody plants made up 59.4% of detected dietary sequences. Forbs contributed 33.6%. Sample richness rose with food availability, and selection shifted with seasonal resources. These local sequence proportions are not a universal diet ratio or a measure by food mass.

Groups are fluid rather than fixed family units: mixed herds include cows, calves and young, while bulls may gather in small groups or stay alone. Individuals join and leave; bison alternate feeding, resting and rumination. In a 1976–1990 Białowieża study, bulls were solitary in 62% of observations, and bull groups were smaller during the rut than before it.

The rut occurs in late summer and autumn; gestation lasts about 254–277 days, with births usually occurring from May to July. A cow leaves the herd to give birth and returns with her calf after several days. Calves may suckle beyond their first year. Cows usually bear one calf about every second year in free-ranging herds; first birth is generally around age four. Bulls join female-and-young groups during the August–September breeding period and move between them while seeking cows.

Grazing removes plant biomass and can open space for other plants; bison also create small disturbed patches and disperse seeds. An eight-year Danish study found higher vascular-plant richness under grazing in old oak and Norway spruce forest, with no response in closed-canopy beech. Effects were strongest where ground vegetation was dense; bryophytes also increased. The result shows context-dependent habitat engineering, not a universal biodiversity gain.

The species became extinct in the wild in 1927; reintroductions began in the 1950s. IUCN’s global assessment published on 10 December 2020 classified it as Near Threatened. A 2022 conservation plan reported c. 6,800 free-ranging animals, c. 500 semi-free and c. 1,700 in ex-situ facilities by 2020—separate categories. Descendants of only 12 founders retain low genetic diversity, and herds remain fragmented. The estimate covered 47 free-ranging subpopulations in 10 countries. The official pedigree book recorded 12,209 animals on 31 December 2024: 9,762 free-living, 722 semi-free and 1,725 captive. These dated records are not a new assessment of extinction risk.

Black-headed Gull
Chroicocephalus ridibundus

The Black-headed Gull breeds widely across Europe and northern Asia, with a small population on Canada’s east coast. Many birds from colder regions migrate south or west for winter, while populations in mild areas may remain.

Adults are about 34–39 cm long, span 100–110 cm and usually weigh 166–400 g; males average heavier, though sexes overlap. The breeding hood is chocolate brown, not black; in winter the head is white with a dark spot behind each eye, and the red bill and legs, black wingtips and white wing edge remain useful marks.
It breeds and feeds on coastal and inland wetlands, including marshes, reedbeds, lakes, ponds and estuaries. Gravel pits, reservoirs, settling ponds, fields and towns also host birds.

This flexible omnivore eats aquatic and terrestrial insects, earthworms and other invertebrates, as well as fish, rodents, seeds, grain, berries and discarded food. In fields it may stamp the ground with webbed feet to bring worms to the surface. At water margins it takes prey from the surface or dips its head below.
During breeding, adults mob birds that threaten eggs or chicks, but dense flocks may flee falcons attacking adults.

In spring, pairs form through visual displays and calls; courtship includes the male regurgitating food for the female before mating. The pair then defends a small territory within its colony. Both adults build a shallow nest from vegetation, twigs and other plant matter, usually in a marsh, reedbed or island, and sometimes on an artificial raft. A usual clutch contains two or three eggs, incubated by both adults for about 23–26 days. The downy chicks leave the nest soon after hatching but depend on their parents, which guard and feed them by regurgitating food onto the ground for the brood. Young usually fledge at 34–36 days and reach breeding maturity around two years.
In Dutch colonies, gulls sometimes defend Sandwich Tern nests from predators, yet also steal tern fish and eat their eggs and chicks.

The global assessment is Least Concern, although regional trends differ. British coastal breeding populations declined between the 1998–2002 and 2015–2021 censuses, with several pressures involved; avian influenza subsequently caused further mortality in 2022–2023.

Black Kite
Milvus migrans

The black kite is a medium-sized, fork-tailed bird of prey, largely a scavenger, with a very wide range. Most northern populations migrate to Africa for the winter, while tropical birds often stay put. In Britain it is only a rare visitor, typically seen in April and May.

It measures about 47–60 cm, with a wingspan of 140–150 cm; females are slightly larger. The plumage is mostly brown, with a paler head, a yellow cere, a dark hooked bill and yellow legs with black talons. The tail is forked, though less deeply than the red kite’s, and the bird looks more uniformly dark. Young birds are lighter and have a shorter fork. Published weights vary, from roughly 0.5 kg to over 0.8 kg.

It favours open country near water, such as rivers, lakes, ponds and wetlands, but also uses woodland, open savanna and even large cities where food is plentiful. It is rarely found in deserts, high mountains or dense forest.

Mainly a scavenger, it eats carrion, including roadkill and refuse, but also takes fish, insects, reptiles, amphibians, small mammals and birds. It finds food by soaring on thermals and has been seen hovering over fires to catch fleeing insects.

The black kite is often sociable, though pairs are more solitary while breeding. It is territorial around its roost and calls loudly with high-pitched notes. Pairs perform aerial courtship in March, including a display in which they lock talons and spiral towards the ground.

Eggs are laid in April and May, usually two or three, and the female incubates them for about 32 days while the male brings food. The nest is a bulky platform of sticks lined with soft material, built by both parents in a tree, on a cliff edge or on a pylon. Chicks stay in the nest for 42–56 days, and birds mature at two to three years.

As an efficient scavenger, it helps break down dead animals. Humans are its main source of mortality, mostly unintentionally, through collisions with vehicles and the ingestion of poisoned items; other black kites sometimes steal eggs from its nests.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern because of its wide range and large population. Some local populations are declining because of water pollution, agricultural pesticides, hunting and poisoning of carcasses. In the UK it is a rare vagrant, with no current population data and no routine monitoring.

Black-legged poison frog
Phyllobates bicolor

This poison frog is native to Colombia’s Pacific-facing Chocó forests, where it walks and hops through damp leaf litter. Its striking yellow or orange body and dark limbs warn predators of defensive skin alkaloids.

Reported adult lengths vary by source, around 32–43 millimetres from snout to vent; females are usually slightly larger. The back and upper limbs are golden yellow to orange, while the legs are mainly black, sometimes spotted blue or gold. Four forelimb fingers and five hind toes have adhesive tips for climbing.

It inhabits humid tropical forests on Colombia’s Pacific slope, from Chocó to western Andean foothills. Records span roughly 400–1,500 metres; it shelters and forages in damp leaf litter near streams.

Adults hunt tiny leaf-litter arthropods, including ants, termites and small beetles, snapping them up with a long, sticky tongue. Tadpoles feed on insect larvae and detritus. Defensive alkaloids in wild frogs are acquired from food rather than manufactured by the frog, although the precise dietary source of batrachotoxin remains unresolved.
By day it moves in short hops, foraging on the forest floor. Males call with trills or buzzes, and rivals may wrestle over calling sites.

Breeding occurs in the rainy season. After courtship, the female lays about 4–30 eggs in a moist sheltered place; fertilization is external, and a parent guards the clutch. At hatching, a parent carries tadpoles on its back to small pools, where they feed and metamorphose before returning to land.

Batrachotoxin is a steroidal alkaloid neurotoxin: it holds voltage-gated sodium channels open, disrupting electrical signals in nerves, muscles and the heart. The frog stores defensive compounds in skin glands; wild frogs carry them, whereas captive-bred frogs generally lack detectable batrachotoxins when their food lacks the relevant alkaloids.

The IUCN Red List assessment published in 2017 classified the species as Endangered. Forest conversion and degradation, including clearing, farming, mining and pollution, threaten its restricted Colombian range.

Black rat
Rattus rattus

The black rat, also called the roof or ship rat, is a small, adaptable rodent whose fortunes have travelled with people. The IUCN assessment describes its original range as Indomalayan; maritime trade carried it far beyond that region, and established populations now occur on many continents and islands. It thrives in settlements as well as forests, so “house rat” describes an association, not a habitat limit.

A black rat is usually slender, with a pointed muzzle, prominent thin ears and a tail longer than its head and body together. Coat colour is variable: animals may be blackish, charcoal, brown or lighter above, often paler below. The brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) is generally heavier and stockier, with a shorter, thicker tail and a blunter muzzle. Colour alone is unreliable, and young rats can be hard to identify.

This species uses warm coastal districts, farms, gardens, woodland and buildings, especially where food and shelter occur together. Its climbing ability makes shrubs, tree crowns, vines, fences, wires and roof spaces accessible; nests can be built above ground in vegetation or structures. In California, roof rats often nest in trees and dense landscaping, but also descend to the ground to forage or feed within trees. They may burrow or use ground-level shelter when elevated sites are scarce, so arboreality is a tendency rather than a rule.

Black rats eat a broad range of foods, usually with a strong plant component: fruit, berries, seeds, nuts, grain, leaves and other vegetation. They also take invertebrates and, where available, eggs or small animals. In four Galápagos petrel colonies sampled on San Cristóbal in June 2013, stomach contents were mostly plant material and arthropods; seeds of the native tree Miconia robinsoniana were especially common. That snapshot is local and seasonal, not a universal menu. The species can shift toward foods that are abundant at a particular site.

Black rats are mainly active at night, when darkness helps them forage while reducing exposure to many daytime predators. They are not invariably solitary: species accounts report groups containing several males and females, with dominance affecting access to mates and defended food territories. The available descriptions do not establish one social structure for every population. Calls, scent deposits and postures provide cues during social contact. Daily routes link nests to food patches, running along branches, fences and overhead lines as well as across the ground.

Where food and shelter remain available, black rats can breed repeatedly; gestation is short, about three to four weeks, and a litter commonly contains several young. Newborns are helpless, naked and blind. The mother nurses and protects them in a nest; fur and mobility develop during the first weeks, and weaning follows after roughly three to four weeks. Young may become reproductively mature within a few months, allowing numbers to rebound quickly. Yet reproduction is not equally continuous everywhere: a 2024 study across Madagascar found strong seasonal variation inside and outside homes, associated partly with rainfall, habitat and rat density.

The rat’s climbing and omnivory connect it to food webs both above and below ground. It may disperse some seeds after eating fruit, but it also consumes seeds and can damage seedlings; whether its net effect benefits a plant depends on the species and setting. In Sydney’s urban bushland remnants, a field experiment found that black rats attacked bird nests, adding a source of nest mortality where they had replaced native bush rats. Their greater use of trees, aided by a longer tail that improves balance, can expose arboreal nests and other tree-dwelling animals to predation.

The amended IUCN global assessment, published in 2021 from an assessment dated 7 September 2016, lists the species as Least Concern because it is widespread and abundant. This global category does not mean harmless: introductions can severely affect local wildlife. On Lord Howe Island, Australia, the black rat arrived after a shipwreck in 1918; a 2000 state scientific determination linked it to losses of endemic birds and the disappearance of the Lord Howe Island stick insect from the main island, threats to native land snails, and reduced palm seed yields. Management concerns are therefore local ecosystem impacts, not global extinction risk. The Island Board’s November 2025 final report confirmed successful rodent eradication and emphasized continued biosecurity to prevent reintroduction.

Black rhinoceros
Diceros bicornis

The black rhinoceros is a large African mammal that browses shrubs and woody plants. Its hooked, grasping upper lip distinguishes it from the square-lipped, grass-grazing white rhinoceros. Both species are generally grey; colour does not explain their common names.

Adults stand about 1.4–1.8 metres at the shoulder. Their thick skin is nearly hairless, and they carry two keratin horns, usually with the front one longer. The pointed, flexible upper lip grasps leaves and twigs. Soil and wallowing can change the apparent skin shade; neither species has a black or white coat.

Its fragmented range lies in eastern and southern Africa. It uses semi-arid scrub, savanna, woodland and forest edges, where browse is available; water access also matters, though succulent plants provide moisture. In Namibia it inhabits arid north-western landscapes. Local habitat conditions influence the area each animal uses.

It browses leaves, shoots, twigs, thorny shrubs and sometimes fruit; grass is occasional rather than its main fare. The prehensile lip gathers branches and guides them to cheek teeth for grinding. Food choices vary with local vegetation and season, so a plant list from one reserve is not universal.

They are often solitary, though females may stay with calves and temporary groups occur. Rhinos feed and travel more in cool morning and evening hours, resting in shade or mud during midday heat. Urine and dung scent marks signal presence and can mark a range; wallowing also cools the body.

After courtship and 15–17 months of gestation, a female gives birth to one calf in a sheltered place. The newborn can usually stand within hours. It stays with its mother for about two to four years, nursing and learning to browse. Long birth intervals slow population recovery after losses.

Browsing removes leaves and twigs and can shape woody vegetation where rhinos feed. The effect depends on local animal density and plant communities, so it is not identical across habitats. Dung piles also carry scent information used by other rhinos.

The IUCN assessment published in 2020 classified the species as Critically Endangered; this dated category is not a new count. Poaching for horn, habitat loss and fragmentation, and insecurity threaten populations. Protected areas, anti-poaching work and carefully planned moves to suitable sites support recovery, though slow reproduction makes losses hard to reverse.

Black Stork
Ciconia nigra
The black stork is a shy, large stork of quiet forests and wetlands. It breeds across the Palearctic from Spain to China and, in most populations, migrates south for the winter.

A bird stands 95–100 cm tall, spans 144–155 cm and weighs about 3 kg. The plumage is black with a green and purple gloss, with a white breast and belly. The bill and legs are scarlet red, brighter in the breeding season and duller in winter. Young birds are duller than adults.

It inhabits old, undisturbed, open forests from sea level to mountains at about 2,000–2,500 m. It forages in shallow streams, pools, marshes and damp meadows, and generally avoids large bodies of water and dense forest. The nest is a large stick structure 4–25 m up in a big tree, or on cliffs in Spain.
It is mainly a fish-eater, but it also takes amphibians, insects, snails, crabs, small reptiles, small mammals and birds. It hunts by sight, often standing in shallow water.

Outside the breeding season it is shy and mostly solitary, and it nests alone, with pairs rarely closer than about one kilometre. It migrates singly or in small groups of up to about 100 birds, along well-defined routes. Some populations, such as those in Spain, do not migrate.

In a study in Dadia National Park, north-eastern Greece (2006–2008), eggs were laid on average on 8 April, the mean clutch was 3.9 eggs, and pairs that succeeded raised an average of 3.26 young. Both parents build the nest and incubate, which takes about 32–38 days, and young fledge at 63–71 days. Maturity comes at 3–5 years.

The species commonly reuses its nests from year to year and may take over nests built by other birds. Large old trees with strong canopies are a limiting resource, and the birds depend on clean streams and wetlands for food. In Greece, small-scale farming that created shallow feeding grounds helped the local population to increase.

The 2015 European assessment by BirdLife International rated it Least Concern, with 9,800–13,900 pairs in Europe and an increasing trend. The main threat is habitat degradation, including loss of large nesting trees, dams and drainage, with hunting in southern Europe and collisions with power lines as further causes of death.

Blackbird
Turdus merula

The Eurasian Blackbird is a thrush in the family Turdidae, native to Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia. The Himalayan, Indian and Chinese blackbirds are separate species. Its flexible diet and ability to use wooded edges, scrub and gardens help it live in both rural and urban landscapes.

An adult is about 25 centimetres long. Adult UK ringing samples averaged 101.8 grams, with the central 90 percent between 87 and 122 grams. The adult male is glossy black with a yellow-orange bill and eye-ring; the female is dark brown with a paler throat and faintly mottled breast, while young birds are browner and more spotted before males acquire adult plumage.

The species uses deciduous and mixed woods, scrub, orchards, hedges and gardens, especially where low vegetation offers cover beside open ground for feeding. Introduced populations established in Australia and New Zealand are geographically separate from the native range.

An opportunistic omnivore, the Blackbird walks or hops over soil, then probes or turns leaves to uncover prey. Earthworms and other invertebrates dominate much of the breeding-season diet, supplying protein to growing chicks; beetles, caterpillars, spiders and small snails add variety. In a Budapest park, parents brought mostly earthworms to early broods in April and May; as June dried and worms became less available, males ranged farther and carried a wider variety of invertebrates. In autumn and winter, berries and other fruits become especially useful, though worms remain available in mild, wet weather.

During breeding, pairs defend territories. Males sing from exposed perches; playback experiments show that song intensity and form can predict escalation in a territorial encounter. Short rattling calls serve in alarm and territorial interactions. Outside the breeding season, birds may gather loosely at rich fruit sources. Migration is partial: a seven-year German study tracked both residents and southbound migrants. Some winter departures occurred during cold spells with snow; cold, snow and reduced food were proposed as possible triggers.

In Portugal, males generally begin singing in February or March to defend territories and attract females. The female builds a sturdy cup of grass, leaves and mud, usually low in vegetation, and lays blue-green, speckled eggs. In the United Kingdom, first clutches are laid on average in late April, typically contain three to four eggs, and two or three broods are common. The female incubates for about 12–14 days. Both parents feed the helpless hatchlings. Young usually leave the nest at about two weeks, before they can forage well; Oxford observations found that parents divide fledgling care, and young generally become independent 15–24 days after fledging.

By eating fruit and later depositing seeds in droppings, Blackbirds can disperse some plants away from the parent; experiments with captive birds show gut passage can alter germination timing, with effects varying by plant species. Blackbirds are also prey for raptors such as Eurasian Sparrowhawks. In a UK urban-park study, magpie predation on Blackbird nests was inferred from disappearance patterns around artificial eggs, rather than directly observed.

The global IUCN Red List update published in 2024 lists the Blackbird as Least Concern, reflecting its large range and population. BTO data show a 21% decline in the UK breeding population between 1967 and 2024, despite partial recovery since the mid-1990s; regional trends differ, including a marked decline in London. A 2022 study associated the 2020 Usutu virus incursion in Greater London with potential impacts on wild birds; later BTO analysis identifies reduced Blackbird survival linked to the virus in recent south-east English declines.

Eurasian Blue Tit
Cyanistes caeruleus
The Eurasian Blue Tit is a small, agile member of the tit family, recognizable by its blue-and-yellow plumage. It ranges across much of Europe and into western Asia.

Adults measure about 11.5–12 centimetres and weigh roughly 10–12 grams; a short, fine bill picks small prey while strong feet grip twigs and leaves. The adult has a blue crown, wings and tail, white cheeks crossed by a dark eye stripe, a greenish back and a yellow underside. The sexes look much alike to human eyes, but ultraviolet reflection on the crown differs between them and can be seen by the birds themselves. Recently fledged young are duller, with pale yellow rather than white cheeks; their post-juvenile moult replaces body feathers within weeks.

The range runs from the British Isles and northern Europe east to the Urals, and south through much of Europe to northwestern Iran. Deciduous and mixed woods offer leafy crowns rich in insects and holes for nesting; orchards, hedgerows, wooded parks and gardens can serve the same purposes where mature trees remain.

For most of the year, Blue Tits glean insects, spiders and other small arthropods from leaves, buds and twigs. Gleaning means taking prey directly from a surface; the bird probes cracks, turns leaves or hangs upside down to reach their undersides, using its feet to steady itself among flexible branches. In spring, soft caterpillars are valuable food for growing nestlings and parents also bring other arthropods. As insects decline in winter, seeds and berries supplement the diet, and feeders provide another source in settled areas.

In spring, the male’s repeated song helps advertise a territory and attract a mate. Contact calls keep nearby birds in touch, while a rough, chattering scold draws attention to danger. In winter, adults and young join mixed-species flocks that search through woodland together; these roaming flocks differ from the family groups formed by dependent fledglings. After leaving the nest, young follow and beg from their parents until they can feed independently.

The female chooses a cavity in a tree, wall or nest box and builds a cup of moss and dry fibres, lined with hair or feathers. British clutches commonly hold eight to ten eggs. The female incubates for about 13–14 days, while the male often brings her food. Both parents then deliver frequent small prey to nestlings, which grow rapidly and usually fledge at about 18–21 days in Britain.

By eating caterpillars and other arthropods, Blue Tits prey on animals that feed on leaves and buds. The seasonal rise in caterpillars can coincide with the heavy food demand of growing chicks, but laying begins earlier and breeding need not match a single peak exactly. In a primeval forest study, caterpillars remained important in nestling diets despite a greater-than-tenfold fall in their supply between years, and only some broods were close to the caterpillar peak.

The British Trust for Ornithology lists the species globally as Least Concern. In Europe, the Red List assessment dated 18 December 2020 and published in 2021 also classified it as Least Concern; it estimated 59.7–95.1 million mature birds and a regional increasing trend. In the United Kingdom, breeding abundance rose by a net 20 percent from 1967 to 2024, with a shallow decline within that longer trend since about 2008.

Blue whale
Balaenoptera musculus

The blue whale is a baleen-bearing rorqual that captures prey with an expandable throat. It occurs in every ocean except the Arctic, but its movements and population structure vary by region. Song, sightings and genetic data distinguish several population units across this wide range.

Its long, tapered body is mottled blue-grey, with a broad U-shaped head and a small dorsal fin far back. Each whale’s stable mottling can help identify it in photographs. Antarctic whales can reach about 33.5 metres and around 150 tonnes; northern whales about 27 metres, with females generally larger than males. About 60–88 pleats run beneath the jaw to the navel, expanding the throat during feeding. Dark, fringed baleen plates hang from the upper jaw and retain krill while water is pushed out.

Blue whales follow krill concentrations, often in productive high-latitude waters during the warm season. Many move toward lower latitudes in winter, but the pattern varies: some Antarctic whales remain south and a northern Indian Ocean population is considered resident, though its movements are poorly known. Eastern North Pacific whales commonly feed off western North America and winter near Mexico and Central America; calves are seen in the Gulf of California. Antarctic, Indian Ocean and Pacific groups are distinguished by sightings, acoustics and genetics, but some regions remain under-sampled.

Krill, especially euphausiid crustaceans, supplies nearly all blue whale food, with prey species varying by region. At a dense patch, a whale accelerates, opens its jaws and engulfs prey and water; its throat pleats stretch around the expanded pouch. It then closes its mouth and presses water through the baleen with its tongue; krill remain caught on the fringed plates and are swallowed. This lunge-and-filter method is costly, but tag-based models show that energy gained per lunge rises sharply with krill density. Dense prey patches help build fat reserves used to fuel migration and reproduction.

Blue whales are usually alone or in pairs; large feeding aggregations are rare. Their low-frequency calls include long tonal notes and repeated songs; researchers have described nine regional song types, several stable for more than 30 years. In a Northeast Pacific study combining tags and acoustic records, foraging whales sang mainly at night, while the population-level transition to migration brought more daytime song. This diel shift is a useful acoustic indicator of migration in that population; whether distant songs guide individual departures remains a hypothesis.

Females usually bear one calf, with pregnancy estimated at 10–12 months and births about every two to three years. Northern births occur mainly in winter; calves are also regularly seen in the Gulf of California. Newborns are several metres long and nurse on their mother’s rich milk for about six to eight months, sometimes while travelling toward feeding areas. Females provide the known parental care, and sparse observations mean reproductive timings remain estimates that can vary among populations.

Blue whales are low-level predators that consume abundant krill and may themselves be prey for killer whales. In a laboratory experiment, faeces from pygmy blue whales stimulated photosynthesis and growth in tested phytoplankton species. This evidence comes from one subspecies under experimental conditions and does not quantify effects in the open ocean or across all populations.

Mechanized harpoons and factory ships made blue whales targets of industrial whaling in the early twentieth century. The IWC records 37,000 whales killed in Antarctica in 1931, most of them blue whales; a global commercial-whaling moratorium began in 1986. For Antarctic blue whales, the IWC’s 2024 estimate is about 4,000 animals (range 1,870–8,400), or 1.9% (range 0.7–4.8%) of estimated pre-whaling abundance. Numbers have risen since the last recorded catches in 1973, yet this estimate shows continued severe depletion. The 2018 IUCN global assessment lists the species as Endangered. The IUCN’s November 2018 update lists the Antarctic subspecies as Critically Endangered. Current pressures include ship strikes, fishing-gear entanglement, underwater noise and climate-related changes to krill habitat.

Bluethroat
Luscinia svecica

The bluethroat is a small, shy, robin-like chat that breeds in damp scrub from Scandinavia across Siberia and winters far to the south. In Britain it is a rare vagrant, seen mostly on migration, with only occasional breeding.

About 13–14 cm long, an adult weighs roughly 17 g and has a wing length near 75 mm. The male’s bright blue throat and chest is bordered by black, white and chestnut bands, with a central spot that is white or chestnut depending on the form. Females are duller, with less blue. The upperparts are brownish grey and the tail has a rusty-red base, with a pale stripe above the eye.

It breeds in the north in Scandinavia and Siberia, extending across Asia towards the Himalayas, and in scattered parts of central and western Europe and around the Black Sea. It prefers willow thickets on damp ground and stays hidden in dense vegetation.

It feeds mainly on insects and other invertebrates, picked from stems and leaves or from under dead leaves on the ground, and only rarely catches insects in the air. It occasionally takes snails and earthworms, and eats seeds and fruit in winter.

A shy, secretive bird, it often flicks into the cover of a bush, flashing the chestnut patches at the base of its tail. Western populations winter in the Mediterranean basin and northern Africa, and eastern ones in the Indian subcontinent.

The deep cup nest of twigs, grass stems and moss, lined with animal hair, is built by the female and hidden in a grass tuft or shrub; nesting runs from May to July. There are typically one or two broods of five to seven eggs (up to nine). The female incubates for 14–15 days and the chicks fledge after about 14–15 days.

As a predominantly insect-eating bird of damp thickets, it feeds on invertebrates in the breeding season and switches partly to seeds and fruit in winter. The species shows great variation in the intensity of its blue throat and in the colour and shape of its throat spot.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern. In the UK it is a rare vagrant, with only about 5,000 BTO records, no population estimate and occasional breeding (the latest cited in 2016); it is protected under Schedule 1 and is Amber-listed by the RSPB.

Bonobo
Pan paniscus

The bonobo (Pan paniscus) is a great ape found only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, south of the Congo River. It shares Pan with the common chimpanzee (P. troglodytes). Communities forage in changing subgroups, with social patterns that vary between them.

Adults are slender, long-legged apes with black hair and dark skin on face, hands and feet. Crown hair often parts centrally; infants have a white rump tuft. Pink lips and a less projecting muzzle distinguish them from the more robust common chimpanzee.

The range lies in the central Congo Basin, between the Congo River and Kasai–Sankuru system, within the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Bonobos use lowland primary, secondary and swamp forests; some also inhabit forest–savanna mosaics. Habitat varies locally.

Bonobos mainly eat fruit, plus leaves, shoots and flowers; insects and small vertebrates are also recorded. Diet varies by site and season. At LuiKotale, fruit appeared in 66% of feeding sessions in one habituated community. They forage in trees and on the ground.

Communities split into temporary parties that later separate or reunite, a fission–fusion pattern. Females often leave their birth community at maturity; males usually stay. Females cooperate around food, but aggression and competition also occur. Patterns vary between sites: bonobos are not universally peaceful.

Females usually have one infant after about eight months of pregnancy. They nurse and carry it for a long period, with births years apart. At Wamba, the mean interval between live births was 4.8 years; individual timing varies. Mothers care for young as they learn to travel and feed.

After eating fruit, bonobos deposit seeds in dung away from parent trees. At LuiKotale, researchers recorded over 91 plant species and a mean dispersal distance of 1.2 kilometres; gut-passed seeds germinated better in trials. This supports a local role in forest regeneration.

The IUCN’s 2016 global assessment classified bonobos as Endangered, citing hunting, habitat loss and degradation, and weak law enforcement. The Bonobo Conservation Initiative also reports human encroachment and disease risk. Population estimates are difficult; this assessment is not a new census.

Common bottlenose dolphin
Tursiops truncatus

The common bottlenose dolphin is a toothed whale of temperate and tropical seas worldwide, found in coastal and offshore waters. In the western North Atlantic, the coastal form is recognized as a separate species, Tursiops erebennus, by the Society for Marine Mammalogy’s 2026 list. Boundaries between species in this genus remain under study. Tursiops aduncus, the Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin, is another distinct species.

Adults are robust, usually grey above and paler below, with a short thick rostrum and curved dorsal fin; coastal individuals tend to be smaller and lighter than offshore ones. Teeth are numerous, conical and suited to seizing prey rather than chewing: each upper jaw side bears about 20–26 and each lower side 18–24. The tail flukes are horizontal, the pectoral flippers broad and rounded, and the dorsal fin falcate; the blowhole opens at the top of the head.

The species uses estuaries, bays, lagoons, harbours, continental shelves and open ocean in temperate and tropical waters. Long-term photo-identification in Sarasota Bay documents a resident, multigenerational community with strong site fidelity; this local pattern does not define every population. NOAA lists nearshore T. erebennus from New York to Florida; its wider range is unresolved.

The diet includes locally available fish, squid and crustaceans. Dolphins locate prey by passive listening and echolocation, especially useful when visibility is poor. Air moving through nasal passages activates the phonic lips to produce brief clicks; forehead tissues including the melon shape and direct the outgoing sonar beam. Echoes are received through sound-sensitive tissues associated with the lower jaw and carry information about target direction and distance. At Cedar Key, Florida, observers recorded group hunting with role specialization: a driver herded fish toward waiting dolphins.

Groups split and reunite, a fission–fusion pattern in which associations change with activity and circumstance. At Sarasota Bay, long-term studies of T. truncatus describe stable male pairs that cooperate in associations accompanying females; these findings are specific to that population. Dolphins produce echolocation clicks as well as whistles and burst-pulsed sounds. Individuals develop learned, distinctive signature whistles. Playback experiments found wild dolphins responded to copies of their own signature whistle, supporting its use as an identity signal directed to another dolphin. During sleep, EEG recordings show slow-wave sleep in one brain hemisphere at a time; dolphins continue surfacing to breathe while the other hemisphere remains more alert.

Females usually give birth to one calf after about 12 months of gestation; NOAA reports births three to six years apart on average in the populations summarized by its account. A Sarasota Bay study found that calving intervals vary with maternal age and calf survival, illustrating that reproductive timing is not constant. Mothers that successfully raised a calf remained associated with it for about 4.2–4.4 years on average, extending well beyond nursing and allowing time for learning and development.

Dolphins are linked to the habitats supporting their prey. In Sarasota Bay, Florida, stomach contents of stranded resident dolphins contained fish, most associated to varying degrees with seagrass. The principal prey produced sounds, suggesting that passive listening helped locate them. Seagrass meadows were important feeding habitat for this community, although animals also foraged elsewhere. Protecting these habitats therefore matters for local dolphin conservation; prey composition and habitat use differ among populations.

The global IUCN assessment dated 13 May 2018 and published in 2019 classified T. truncatus as Least Concern; that category does not establish the condition of every local population. NOAA lists several western North Atlantic coastal stocks as depleted under US management and reports unknown trends for many other stocks. Documented pressures include bycatch and entanglement, vessel strikes, pollution, harmful algal toxins, habitat alteration and underwater noise; status depends on population and region.

Brown bear
Ursus arctos

The brown bear ranges widely across Eurasia and North America, from forests and mountains to tundra and coasts. Separated populations differ in size, coat, seasonal routines, and food choices according to local conditions. In North America, the grizzly is a brown bear subspecies within this same species.

Adults have a heavy body, muscular shoulder hump, and long foreclaws for digging. Their coat ranges from blond or pale brown to dark brown or black; pale tips on guard hairs can look grizzled. They walk plantigrade, with the whole foot on the ground.

The species occupies forests, shrublands, grasslands, wetlands, and other terrestrial habitats. In Alaska, bears use low slopes and wetlands for spring greens, berry openings in summer, then salmon rivers or alpine berry patches in autumn. Seasonal movements follow food.

Brown bears are omnivores, eating grasses, roots, berries, nuts, fish, insects, small mammals, carrion, and sometimes larger prey. Yellowstone examples include trout, elk calves, roots, berries, and pine seeds; coastal Alaskan bears can exploit salmon runs.

In Yellowstone, grizzlies are usually solitary outside courtship, family groups, or concentrated foods; some gather at streams, carcasses, or moth aggregations. They den through winter, though timing and emergence vary with sex and reproductive status.

In Yellowstone, mating is from mid-May to mid-July. After delayed implantation, cubs are born in dens in late January or February, usually one to three per litter, occasionally four. They nurse through winter and generally stay with their mother about two years.

In Alaska, seasonal movements bring bears to salmon streams and berry patches in turn; accumulated fat helps support winter denning. These rich feeding sites may attract many bears to one place, particularly where food is abundant.

The IUCN SSC Bear Specialist Group reports the species has been globally Least Concern since 1996 and is stable overall. This masks threatened isolated populations and past range losses. A 2023 European update reported recovery and expansion in several large populations.

European hare
Lepus europaeus

The European hare is a large, ground-dwelling lagomorph of open country across much of Europe and western Asia. Unlike rabbits, it does not shelter in a communal burrow: it rests in a shallow surface hollow and depends on concealment, keen senses and rapid flight. Its life is closely tied to the seasonal food and cover of grasslands and farmland.

Adults are typically tawny or reddish brown, with paler flanks, a light underside and a black upper surface to the tail. The long ears have dark tips; the hind legs are much longer and more powerful than the forelegs. These proportions support fast running and sharp turns across open ground. Compared with a European rabbit, a hare is larger, longer-legged and lacks the rabbit’s burrow-dwelling build.

The species uses grassland, pasture, arable fields and other open or lightly covered ground. Hares remain above ground through the year. A resting hollow, called a form, may lie among grasses or crop plants, in a dry sheltered patch or on a slight rise. The animal presses into the hollow with its ears laid back, so its outline is difficult to see; it does not excavate a warren like a rabbit.

This herbivore eats grasses, wild herbs and crops, with the available menu changing through the year. In an Austrian arable study, hares selected forage richer in energy, fat and protein and lower in fibre; they also used weeds and grasses rather than relying only on crops. When green food is scarce, woody shoots and bark can enter the diet. Like other leporids, hares ferment plant material in the caecum and re-ingest soft caecal droppings, recovering nutrients from this hindgut digestion.

Hares are mostly solitary, though several may feed in the same open area. They spend much of the day at or near a form and forage mainly at night or around twilight. When disturbed, a hare can burst from cover and run at high speed, using long hind legs and abrupt changes of direction to evade pursuit. Springtime boxing is often a female striking an insistent courting male with her forepaws, rather than two males fighting.

In Central Europe, breeding can extend from winter into autumn. Females may produce several litters, with litter size varying by season and commonly one to four in the cited regional studies. Leverets are precocial: they are born furred, with eyes open, and can move soon after birth. The mother leaves them concealed apart from brief nursing visits, usually once each night; this limits the time adults gather at a vulnerable litter. Weaning occurs at about five weeks.

By grazing selectively, hares use both wild vegetation and cultivated plants, while their feeding can affect young crops and woody growth. They are also prey, particularly when young: foxes are an important predator in parts of Europe. Their dependence on both food and hiding cover makes the arrangement of fields matter. Studies in Germany show that harvest and other farm operations can change how hares use fields, with responses depending on the management and landscape.

A widespread species can still be scarce locally. The Mammal Society lists the European hare as Least Concern globally, while documenting declines and habitat problems in Britain. This regional picture should not be mistaken for the status of every population. Intensive, specialised farming can reduce the mix of forage and cover, and machinery may kill hares; local outcomes also vary with predation and land use. The broad global category therefore sits alongside substantial regional conservation concern.

Buff-tailed bumblebee
Bombus terrestris

The buff-tailed bumblebee is a large social bee native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia. Its annual colony begins with one queen, grows through worker daughters, then produces males and future queens. People rear it commercially for crop pollination, and escaped colonies have established beyond its native range. European assessments still list it as widespread and Least Concern, a regional status that does not describe impacts after introduction elsewhere.

Adults have dense black fur, two golden-yellow bands and a pale abdomen tip. Queens measure about 20–22 millimetres, workers 11–17 and males 14–16; these British reference ranges vary among individuals. A queen’s tail is buff, while workers and males usually have white tails, sometimes with a fine buff edge. Workers can resemble the white-tailed bumblebee, Bombus lucorum; DNA markers distinguish the species more reliably than some field keys.

The species uses gardens, parks, farmland and meadows where flowers and nest shelter are available. Queens often nest underground in abandoned rodent burrows, reusing their protected cavities. In Britain, queens emerge in late winter or early spring; workers appear about six weeks after a nest is founded.

Adults drink nectar for energy and gather pollen to nourish brood. Their short tongue works well on many open flowers but less well in long tubular blooms; they nevertheless forage as generalists across many plant species. Sometimes a bee pierces a flower’s side to reach nectar without touching its reproductive parts. On nightshades whose anthers release pollen through small pores, workers grip the anthers and vibrate flight muscles, shaking pollen loose into their hairs. The foundress feeds the first larvae; later, workers provision brood as the queen focuses on laying eggs. The nest contains small pots for sugary food, separate from clusters of brood cells. Unlike honeybees, these bumblebees vibrate flowers to release pollen from poricidal anthers. Pollen is also stored for the brood, but nectar and pollen reserves remain relatively small rather than providing a large winter stock.

One mated queen founds the nest alone; her daughters become workers who forage, feed larvae and maintain it, while males mainly leave to seek mates. Colony size varies; British accounts give a broad range of 100 to 1,000 bees. Bumblebees lack the honeybee waggle dance; chemical and contact cues help coordinate activity. Workers can learn floral scents brought home by successful foragers. Flight muscles warm before flight in cool air. At the nest, queens and later workers also generate heat to keep brood warm.

In the usual temperate cycle, a mated queen spends winter in diapause and emerges when conditions allow nesting. Winter-active colonies have been observed in southern Britain, including urban parks and gardens. She lays eggs in a wax-lined nest and incubates them using heat from her flight muscles. Eggs hatch into larvae, which grow, spin cocoons and pupate; laboratory worker development averaged about 26 days from egg to adult, while field timing varies. The first workers take over much of the foraging and brood care. Later the colony produces males and new queens; after mating, the young queens enter diapause and the old colony normally dies.

Foraging bees carry pollen between flowers, making them important pollinators of crops. Some crops benefit from the bee’s abundance and its ability to vibrate poricidal anthers, releasing pollen. Commercial rearing makes it a useful managed pollinator, but introductions can alter local communities. In Chile and Patagonia, surveys recorded introduced B. terrestris spreading as native B. dahlbomii retreated; competition and parasite spillover may contribute, though their relative roles remain unresolved. This regional case is distinct from the species’ widespread, Least Concern status in Europe.

The IUCN assessment dated 14 July 2023 and published in 2025 lists B. terrestris as Least Concern in Europe and the EU27, citing its broad range and continued abundance. This regional status does not remove ecological concerns where commercial colonies escape and establish beyond the native range. A 2013 Patagonian survey reported rapid spread and a marked local replacement pattern involving native B. dahlbomii. A 2014 study detected parasites in introduced and native bees but said the evidence could not assign the decline to one cause. IUCN notes that climate and land-use change could affect the species in Europe in coming decades.

Northern Fur Seal
Callorhinus ursinus

The northern fur seal is an eared seal of the North Pacific that spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore in dense colonies to breed. Most of the population breeds on the Pribilof Islands in the Bering Sea. Males are far larger than females.

It has a stocky body, a small head, a very short snout, small external ears and extremely dense fur. Its fore flippers are the longest of any eared seal. Adult males reach about 2 m and up to 270 kg and are dark brown to black,, while females are about 1.5 m, grey or brown above and paler below. Pups are born black and turn silver-grey after about three months.

It breeds in the Bering Sea and along the eastern North Pacific, on islands such as St. Paul, St. George and Bogoslof in Alaska and on several Russian islands. Outside the breeding season it ranges widely over the North Pacific, the Bering Sea and the Sea of Okhotsk, and in winter reaches as far south as southern California and Honshu in Japan.

It is an opportunistic hunter of midwater fish and squid, and feeds mostly at night. Walleye pollock is the main prey over the Bering Sea shelf, while off the US West Coast it takes mackerel, squid, sardines and anchovies, among others.

It is highly pelagic and mostly solitary at sea, and can stay out in the open ocean for nearly two years before returning to its breeding colonies. On land during the breeding season it is aggressive: males defend territories by pushing and biting, and fights between males can be fatal.

Males return to the breeding islands from May and hold territories, typically from about age 10. Females give birth to a single pup and mate again within about five days. Females usually have their first pup at 5–6 years and are most productive from about 8 to 13. Pups nurse until weaning at about four months.

As a predator of schooling fish and squid, the northern fur seal links the open North Pacific to its breeding islands. It is itself preyed on by killer whales, Steller sea lions and sharks. Pups are taken by Steller sea lions, and entanglement in marine debris and lost fishing gear is a major hazard.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Vulnerable (assessed in 2015). In the US it is protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, and the Pribilof Islands and Eastern Pacific stock was listed as depleted in 1988 after falling by more than half from about 2.2 million seals in the 1950s. Its 2019 abundance estimate was about 627,000, and pup production declined roughly 1.8% a year from 1999 to 2019.
