Canada Goose
Branta canadensis

The Canada Goose is a large, adaptable waterfowl native to North America, from Arctic coasts and tundra to temperate wetlands. Its familiar honking flocks also occupy many cities and farms, where lawns and waste grain provide dependable food. The species varies greatly across its range, with northern forms generally smaller than southern ones. Four especially small forms once included within this species are now treated as the separate Cackling Goose, Branta hutchinsii.

Adults have a black head and long black neck, a broad white patch joining the cheeks beneath the chin, a brown back, pale breast, and black bill and feet. This white chinstrap is a diagnostic band across the lower face and throat, not a wholly white face. Adults measure about 76–110 cm long with a 127–170 cm wingspan, varying geographically. In flight, a white band across the rump contrasts with the dark tail.

The species uses marshes, lakes, rivers, estuaries, coastal bays, and tundra pools, usually where open water lies beside grassy feeding ground. It rests and escapes danger on water, but often obtains most of its food on land. In settled landscapes it readily uses park lawns, golf courses, reservoirs, and harvested fields. Nesting pairs favor islands, shorelines, or other sites with clear views and nearby water, though some urban birds nest on roofs or structures.

Canada Geese are herbivores. They graze leaves and shoots of grasses and sedges, browse aquatic plants, and take seeds, berries, and cultivated crops such as cereal grain and corn. Their broad, flattened bill clips vegetation and strains plant material from shallow water; they may tip forward to reach submerged growth. Short new grass is tender and protein-rich, useful to growing goslings and adults replacing feathers, whereas grain in autumn and winter supplies energy for fat reserves. This flexibility helps them exploit both natural wetlands and agriculture.

Pairs commonly remain together year-round and often for life, joining larger flocks outside the breeding season. Family groups help organize migration: geese travel by day or night in loose flocks, frequently in a V, with individuals taking turns at the front. Honks maintain contact and coordinate movement; head-pumping, hissing, and wing displays warn intruders near nests or feeding sites. Northern breeders generally travel south for winter, while many temperate-breeding populations move little, although young and nonbreeders may travel north to molt, the annual replacement of flight feathers that leaves adults unable to fly for several weeks.

Canada Geese usually begin breeding at two or three years of age. The pair defends a territory, and the female builds a plant-lined ground nest, often close to water; she lays a typical clutch of five to seven eggs and incubates them for about 28–30 days while the male guards nearby. The down-covered goslings hatch with open eyes and leave the nest within a day or two. Both parents attend the nest, and the newly hatched young can walk, swim, and feed soon afterwards. They usually fly at roughly six to seven weeks and may stay with the family through their first year.

Grazing can keep lawns short and transfers plant production into prey for foxes, coyotes, eagles, and other predators, especially when geese are nesting or flightless. On water, families and flocks also share feeding and roosting places with other waterbirds. Their use of cropland and lawns creates close contact with people: concentrated flocks can consume crops, leave droppings, and create aircraft-strike hazards near airports. These effects are strongest where abundant food and safe roosts bring many birds together, rather than being an inevitable result of every goose population.

The Atlantic migratory population fell sharply after approaching one million birds in the 1970s; authorities closed its sport season from 1995 to 1999, and the population later recovered. Its continental abundance is now high, helped by protected nesting sites, urban lawns, and agricultural grain; the archived Canadian status profile records a global Least Concern assessment from 2018. In Britain, the bird was introduced as an ornamental species in the seventeenth century and later expanded following further releases; it is now widespread but remains an introduced population there. Local management addresses crop damage, fouling, and airport safety, while migratory populations continue to be managed through regulated harvest.

Canada lynx
Lynx canadensis

The Canada lynx is a wild cat of northern North America, living in boreal forests from Alaska across Canada and into the northern United States. Its life is closely tied to the snowshoe hare, whose abundance shapes where lynx thrive and how their numbers change.

This medium-sized cat has long legs, broad furred paws, cheek ruffs and narrow black ear tufts. Its short tail ends in black. The coat is usually grayish or buff, sometimes faintly spotted; seasonal fur changes make it look less sleek in summer.

Lynx use a mosaic of forest stands. Dense young growth shelters hares, while older trees, fallen trunks and root mounds provide cover and denning places. In mountain regions, deep winter snow helps define suitable habitat and gives lynx an advantage over some competing predators.

The snowshoe hare is its principal prey, especially in winter. Lynx also take mice, voles, squirrels, grouse and other birds. Alternative foods matter more when hares are scarce or in some southern populations; hungry lynx may roam farther, though substitutes may not nourish them adequately.

Usually solitary, the lynx moves quietly through cover and hunts mainly by sight and hearing, stalking or waiting by prey trails before an ambush. It may be active day or night, often around dawn and dusk. Scent marks and calls help individuals communicate across ranges.

Mating occurs in late winter or early spring. After roughly nine weeks, a female gives birth in a sheltered den among fallen wood. She raises kittens alone. Litter size and breeding success vary with food supply; poor hare years reduce reproduction and kitten survival.

The lynx–hare relationship forms a predator–prey cycle. When hares are plentiful, lynx find food readily; after hare numbers fall, lynx populations usually decline later. Cycle timing and strength differ by region, so northern patterns do not apply everywhere.

Risks vary across its range. Habitat fragmentation, trapping, competition with coyotes or bobcats, and changing snow affect local populations, especially near the southern edge. Canada’s 1989 and 2001 national assessments classified it as not at risk; New Brunswick listed it as special concern in 2022.

Indian Stick Insect
Carausius morosus

The Indian stick insect, also called the laboratory stick insect, is a wingless phasmid that mimics a twig. Native to southern India, it has been kept in culture in Europe since the late 1800s and is now common as a pet and a laboratory animal.

Females measure about 70 to 84 mm in one source and up to roughly 100 mm in another, and are thicker than the shorter, thinner, brown males. The body is stick-like and wingless, coloured dull green to brown, sometimes mottled, with antennae about as long as the legs. Adult females show red patches at the base of the front legs.

The species was first described from Shembagonor and Trichinopoly in southern India, and is also reported from the Palni Hills. Introduced populations are known from Australia, the Azores, Madagascar, Madeira, South Africa, the United Kingdom and the United States, probably from escaped insects and discarded eggs.
It is a plant-eater that feeds on many kinds of plants. In captivity it takes bramble and privet, and in Cape Town suburbs it feeds on ivy.

It is mainly active at night and rests motionless by day, a classic twig mimic that can stay still for hours. When disturbed it may sway from side to side as if moved by wind, drop to the ground, feign death with its body rigid, or release fluid from its mouthparts.

Introduced and cultured populations reproduce by parthenogenesis: unmated females lay eggs that hatch, and males are rare. In India the species is believed to reproduce sexually, at least in part of its range. Females drop several hundred round brown eggs, which hatch after 8 to 15 weeks in one source and 4 to 6 months in another; the nymphs moult six times and mature in about 4 to 7 months.

Where it has been introduced, it can feed on ornamental plants. In California it has been recorded as a pest of ornamentals and is rated high for environmental impact but low as a pest overall. Frosts normally kill it in Britain, although milder winters have helped its numbers.

No global conservation assessment was found. The species is widely kept in culture, and wild status in India is not documented in the sources consulted; elsewhere it is an introduced species rather than one at risk.

European goldfinch
Carduelis carduelis

The European goldfinch is a small finch native to Europe, North Africa and western and central Asia. It uses open country where seed-bearing plants grow near trees or shrubs, including field margins, orchards, villages and gardens. Thistles and teasels are characteristic foods, but it takes seeds from many plants. Some populations remain year-round; others move seasonally. British and Irish records include residents and movements to and from continental Europe.

Adults have a red face, black-and-white head, brown upperparts, pale underparts and broad yellow wing bands. The short pointed bill is pale. The sexes look similar, with subtle differences in facial plumage. Juveniles lack the red, patterned head and instead appear brown and streaked, though they already show the yellow wing band.

Goldfinches feed where herbs can flower and set seed, and nest in trees or shrubs nearby. British and Irish surveys find them in varied breeding habitats, including villages and reedbeds. A study near Sagunto in eastern Spain sampled chicks in intensively cultivated orange-growing country; their food reflected local plants. This single study cannot define habitat use across the species’ range. The recurring requirements are seed heads and woody nesting cover.

Seeds dominate the diet, especially those of thistles, teasels, sow-thistles and dandelions. A slender pointed bill and agile feet help the bird cling to stems and reach seeds in flower heads. A breeding-season study in German orchards found that seed choice reflected availability and energetic profitability; extracting seeds from attached heads required more effort than eating loose seeds.

Goldfinches commonly feed in flocks outside the breeding season, sometimes alongside other finches. Contact calls accompany their movements between feeding areas. The species is a partial migrant: some British birds stay all year, while others move south and northern European birds arrive. Danish ringing recoveries document southwestward autumn movement, including records from the Netherlands, Belgium and France. These individual recoveries do not establish one route for every population.

The female builds a moss, grass and fibre cup in a tree or shrub. BTO records from Britain and Ireland give a usual clutch of five eggs, female incubation for 12–14 days and fledging at roughly two weeks. Two broods are typical in that dataset; three are exceptional. Near Sagunto, a study of 31 nests found that chicks received mainly seeds, plus aphids and beetle larvae; the animal-food contribution declined during the breeding season.

Diet samples establish the goldfinch as a consumer of seeds from many herbs. Near Sagunto, sow-thistle seeds were prominent in chick food; in German orchards adults selected seeds partly according to energetic return. These studies document seed consumption, not a major dispersal role or a measured effect on plant abundance. Seasonal availability of flowering plants influences the food accessible to adults and chicks.

The IUCN’s 2019 global assessment classified the species as Least Concern despite an overall decreasing trend. BirdLife International’s 2021 European Red List classified the species as Least Concern and estimated 56.1–88.7 million mature individuals, with an increasing regional trend. This dated continental assessment does not mean every national population is increasing. BTO monitoring reports long-term increases and range expansion in Britain and Ireland, and considers garden feeding one contributor to recent British growth. Local conservation still depends on regional trends and the availability of seed-bearing plants.

Carrion crow
Corvus corone
The carrion crow is a large, adaptable corvid native to western Europe and parts of eastern Asia.

Adults are about 48–52 cm long, with an 84–100 cm wingspan and a usual mass of roughly 400–600 g; males average somewhat larger, but the sexes look alike. Its plumage is glossy black, and the bill and legs are black. The slimmer-billed adult rook has bare greyish skin at the bill base; the much larger raven has a heavier bill and shaggy throat. The similarly sized hooded crow, Corvus cornix, is a distinct species with a grey body and black head, wings and tail.
Across its broad Eurasian range, the species uses woodland edges, farmland, moorland, coasts and urban parks.
An opportunistic omnivore, it takes seeds, grain, fruit, insects, earthworms, eggs, small animals and food discarded by people. It also scavenges carcasses and picks parasites from livestock.

Breeding pairs defend territories throughout the year, while unpaired birds and young gather in flocks and winter roosts. Calls and postures convey signals. Experiments show that carrion crows recognize individual humans.

The pair builds a deep stick nest, usually high in a tree, in early spring. A typical clutch contains three or four eggs; the female incubates them for about 18–20 days while her mate brings food. Both parents feed the helpless chicks, which leave the nest at roughly 29 days, then continue to depend on adults while learning to forage before becoming independent.
They scavenge carcasses and take invertebrates and small vertebrates, sometimes raiding eggs or chicks; they are both scavengers and active predators.

BirdLife International’s 2021 European Red List classifies the species as Least Concern in Europe, based on national data largely reported in 2019–2020; this is a regional assessment, not a current global reassessment. In France, perceived agricultural damage has led to campaigns of destruction and deterrence.

Domestic cattle
Bos taurus

Taurine cattle are large, hoofed mammals domesticated from aurochs in Southwest Asia. Ancient genomes indicate a small founding group and later mixing with other aurochs lineages as herds spread. Today people keep cattle worldwide in varied production systems.

Cattle have a sturdy body, broad muzzle, cloven hooves and a long tufted tail. Coat, size and horns vary widely among breeds; some are naturally hornless. The term includes both sexes: mature females are cows, males bulls, and young animals calves.

FAO livestock maps show cattle widely distributed around the world. They live in human-managed pastures, mixed farms, extensive pastoral systems, feedlots or barns. Local conditions vary with husbandry, while climate, water and forage shape where herds can be maintained.

Cattle eat grasses, leaves and other plants, then regurgitate partly digested forage to chew it again. Their four digestive compartments are the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. Microbes ferment fibrous plants in the rumen, making their energy available to the animal.

Cattle are social grazers that feed and rest in groups. Studies of managed herds find associations among individuals and different responses to familiar and unfamiliar herd members. They communicate through posture, touch, smell and calls; group composition can affect these relationships.

Females cycle when not pregnant; estrus averages about 21 days between cycles, with variation. A receptive female may stand to be mounted. After fertilization, gestation lasts about 283 days on average and ends with a calf’s birth; the mother then produces milk.

Cattle grazing removes plant shoots; dung and urine return nutrients, while hooves compact soil. In one Finnish dairy pasture, these processes altered plant growth and soil communities. Their effects arose from defoliation, patchy excreta and trampling, and depend on local pasture conditions.

Bos taurus is domesticated and maintained in human herds, rather than a wild population with a natural range. Relevant conservation concerns include preserving domestic breed diversity and locally adapted traits. The extinct aurochs is a separate ancestral wild taxon, not the status of domestic cattle.

Domestic guinea pig
Cavia porcellus

The domestic guinea pig is a small caviid rodent whose populations are primarily maintained by people. The domesticated lineage is recognized as Cavia porcellus, taxonomically distinguished from the wild species C. aperea and C. tschudii. Genetic comparisons identify the Andean montane guinea pig, C. tschudii, as its closest wild relative, while ancient DNA points to a more complex domestication history than a single simple origin. Genomic project accounts place Andean domestication more than four millennia ago. Today people keep guinea pigs as companions and research animals, and raise them for food in parts of South America.

A guinea pig has a compact, low-set body, short limbs, a blunt head and no external tail. Each forefoot has four digits and each hind foot three. Its coat may be short or long, smooth or rough, and comes in many colours and patterns; these differences reflect selective breeding. Smithsonian measurements place typical adults at about 20–25 centimetres long, although size varies among breeds.

Cavia porcellus is associated with human settlements rather than a self-sustaining wild range: it lives in household enclosures, farms and research facilities, and has travelled globally through human keeping and trade. The high Andean grasslands sometimes described as guinea-pig habitat belong to wild relatives, especially C. tschudii, not automatically to the domestic species. That montane cavy is reported from Peru, Bolivia, north-western Argentina and north-eastern Chile.

Guinea pigs are obligate herbivores and hindgut fermenters. Their large caecum contains microbes that process plant fibre after it passes through the stomach and small intestine. One published estimate attributes about 30–40% of maintenance energy to short-chain fatty acids from gut fermentation. Guinea pigs also eat faecal pellets (coprophagy); preventing this behaviour reduces fibre digestion and body weight, although its precise nutritional contribution remains uncertain. The Merck Veterinary Manual states that guinea pigs do not produce cecotropes, the distinct soft pellets associated with caecotrophy. They also cannot synthesize vitamin C: evolutionary research reports loss of the GULO gene, which encodes the final enzyme in the animal pathway.

Guinea pigs are social and commonly remain close to other individuals, resting or huddling together. In domestic groups, males can form dominance relationships. Calls documented in laboratory recordings include purrs and rumbles during interactions between males, with whines and chutters also heard; the sound pattern depended on the social setting, so a call should not be assigned one universal meaning.

Pregnancy lasts about 59–72 days, according to a veterinary-school natural-history account. Pups are born furred, with eyes and ears open; they can stand and move soon after birth and nibble solid food within a day. This precocial development contrasts with the helpless young of many rodents, yet pups still remain attached to their mother. Their early mobility does not mean they are independent at birth.

The domestic guinea pig occupies an ecological setting built around people. In Andean societies, animals are raised in household settings and form part of local food traditions; elsewhere they are kept as pets or used in biomedical research. These uses explain the species’ wide distribution without implying a wild ecological role. Habitat and ecological relationships described for wild cavies belong to those wild species unless independently demonstrated for domestic C. porcellus.

The domestic species is maintained through breeding and is not treated by the Smithsonian National Zoo as a threatened wild animal. That description should not be transferred to C. tschudii or other wild Cavia species: they are separate taxa with their own distributions and conservation evidence. The domestic guinea pig’s global presence does not mean that it has a naturally widespread wild population.

Cercopithecus lomamiensis

The lesula is a guenon of the central Congo forests, described as a new species only in 2012. The first one noticed by scientists was a young pet in the town of Opala in 2007; fieldwork then found it living wild in a forest block that had hardly been explored. It is listed as Vulnerable.

A medium-sized, slim monkey. Measured adult males had a body of 47–65 cm and weighed 4.0–7.1 kg, but only a few animals were measured and no adult female was. It has a long grizzled blond mane, a black back banded with amber, and an amber patch brightest at the base of the tail. Throat and chest are yellowish buff, shoulders and limbs black, thighs silvery grey and the tail black beyond its amber base. The bare face is pale pinkish grey to tan with a cream stripe down the nose, and adult males have a bright blue scrotum and perineum.

It lives in mature upland evergreen humid forest, including forests dominated by Gilbertiodendron, at 400–715 m. It was seen less often in regrowth near villages and never in seasonally flooded forest or savanna gallery forest. Its known range covers about 17,000 km² in central Congo, between the middle Lomami River in the east and the upper Tshuapa River in the west.

It eats leaf stalks, ripe and unripe fruit, flower buds and growing shoots of two ground-living herbs of the arrowroot family, and also picks up food dropped by other primates feeding above. The full diet and its seasonal changes have not been documented.

It is semi-terrestrial: of 48 animals seen, about a third were on the ground when first met, and fleeing animals often ran along the ground. It was usually met alone or in groups of up to five, and in 11 of 19 encounters it was with other monkeys. At dawn, low booming calls given in bouts of two or three are heard over long distances; the callers were almost certainly males.

Almost nothing is documented about its breeding in the wild: season, gestation, litter and lifespan are all unknown. The only detail reported is that young are pale blond overall and that the amber patch on the back appears within their first three months.

It often travels with other monkeys, such as Wolf’s mona monkey, the red-tailed monkey and the red colobus. The only recorded predation was one attack by a crowned eagle. Its ecological role has not been studied.

It is listed as Vulnerable. The main threat is bushmeat hunting, which has grown over the past decade and feeds city markets such as Kindu and Kisangani; its range was not yet logged or mined when it was described. It was the least often seen primate in the surveys, though the authors called it not uncommon in its range. Population size has not been estimated, and a protected area of about 9,000 km² was proposed in 2012.

Fringilla coelebs

The Eurasian chaffinch is a small, widespread finch whose continental range extends from Europe eastward through temperate Asia. AviList 2025b treats Fringilla coelebs as distinct from the African, Azores, Madeira and Canary Islands chaffinches; the Tenerife and Gran Canaria Blue Chaffinches are separate species too. Many populations are resident, while birds from northern and eastern breeding areas move south or west for winter.

Breeding males have a blue-grey crown, rosy face and breast, chestnut back, and two white wing bars. The male’s pinkish-orange breast becomes a darker wine shade in winter, a subtle seasonal change within the same male pattern. The female and juvenile are softer brown and olive tones; their pale wing bars and white outer tail feathers remain useful clues in flight. The RSPB lists a typical adult length of 14.5 cm, a weight range of 18–29 g, and a wingspan of 24.5–28.5 cm. In British ringing samples, males average 22.6 g and females 20.9 g, against 21.8 g for adults overall.
In Britain, chaffinches occupy deciduous, mixed and coniferous woodland during breeding and also visit open farmland in winter.

Outside breeding, adults pick seeds from the ground and rarely take them directly from plants; in spring and summer they also glean insects from shrub and tree foliage. They feed nestlings invertebrates, including caterpillars, spiders, crane flies, aphids, and beetles, shifting the young diet toward animal prey.

During spring, males sing from exposed perches and defend breeding territories; the familiar song descends through a short sequence and ends in a flourish. Chaffinch song is learned from adult tutors, and neighbouring populations develop distinct song dialects through cultural transmission. Outside the territorial season, birds feed in loose flocks, sometimes alongside Bramblings and other finches; migration is partial, with northern and eastern birds moving while many western birds stay year-round.

The female builds a compact, deep cup in a tree or shrub fork, weaving moss, grass, roots, lichens, bark, hair, and feathers together. In Britain, laying begins on average around 30 April; a typical clutch contains four or five eggs, incubated by the female for about 12–13 days. The female feeds nestlings caterpillars and other animal food; after they leave the nest, the male also helps provision the young for about three weeks. BTO nest records show that chicks usually fledge at 13–15.5 days.

On nine south-central English farms, adults made little use of crops when feeding nestlings; trees and hedges, especially oaks and willows, were frequent feeding sites. Successful nests tended to be nearer oaks or willows than nests where chicks starved; in one study year, starvation was less frequent along field boundaries with oak trees.

The IUCN assessment, last assessed on 9 August 2018 and published as an amended 2019 version, listed the then broadly defined Common Chaffinch as Least Concern and reported an increasing global population trend at that time; its preliminary population estimate still required validation. That assessment predates the current separation of several island and North African chaffinch species, so it should not be read as a fresh assessment of every present-day taxon. In the UK, the BTO records a 26% breeding decline (1967–2024), though the species remains Green on the UK Birds of Conservation Concern list; numbers have fallen in all four countries since about 2010 after late-century growth. Trichomonosis, a contagious protozoan disease, has been linked to the downturn, but BTO researchers say its role in the sharper recent decline remains uncertain.

Cheetah
Acinonyx jubatus

The cheetah is a large African and Asian cat, the only living species in genus Acinonyx. Its slim body, long legs and blunt, partly non-retractile claws suit acceleration over open ground. It is mostly solitary, except for mothers with cubs and male coalitions.

An adult has a slender frame, small rounded head and yellowish, tawny or grey coat with separate black spots. Dark tear-lines run from the inner eye corners toward the mouth. Its spotted tail ends in dark rings and a pale tip.

Cheetahs use open habitats where they can see prey and run: African grasslands, savannas and dry country, including deserts. They also occur in open woodland and scrub. Their former range spanned Africa to the Middle East and India; populations now occupy scattered remnants.

It hunts mainly small and medium-sized hoofed mammals, including gazelles and impalas; hares and ground birds supplement its diet. It approaches or watches from cover, then charges and trips prey with its forelegs before suffocating it with a throat bite. Many chases fail.

Females generally roam alone; males may form lasting coalitions, often with brothers, and defend territories. Females do not defend territories. Scent marks and calls maintain contact: mothers call to hidden cubs, while coalition partners vocalize when separated. Cheetahs sometimes climb trees.

Breeding occurs year-round. After about three months of gestation, a female gives birth. Wild litters average fewer cubs than the three to six often reported by zoos. Cubs are helpless and hidden at birth; the mother moves their den and teaches hunting before independence.

The cheetah competes with larger carnivores for food and space. Lions, spotted hyenas and leopards can kill cubs, and competitors sometimes steal its kills. Successful hunting therefore does not always secure a meal; reproduction and cub survival also depend on these interactions.

In its profile consulted in October2026, the IUCN Cat Specialist Group reports the species as Vulnerable. Habitat loss, conflict with livestock owners and illegal trade threaten fragmented populations. Most survivors occur in eastern and southern Africa; the remaining Asiatic population is in Iran.

Chimpanzee
Pan troglodytes

The chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) is a great ape native to tropical Africa. It differs from the bonobo (Pan paniscus), found south of the Congo River; chimpanzees live north of it. This adaptable, social omnivore climbs and travels on the ground, and learns local traditions.

Adults have long arms, a robust build and dark brown to black hair; the face, palms and soles are bare. They have no tail, walk on their knuckles and climb readily. Males are generally larger than females, and coat shade varies.

The range runs from West Africa to western Uganda and Tanzania, interrupted by the Congo basin of the bonobo. Chimpanzees inhabit rainforests, dry forests, woodland-savanna mosaics and mountain forests. Some populations also live in open savanna, so the species is not restricted to dense forest.

Fruit is often a major food, alongside leaves, seeds, flowers, bark, honey and insects; the mix varies by season and place. Chimpanzees also hunt or scavenge vertebrates such as monkeys and small antelopes. Some use probes at termite mounds or tools to fish for ants; techniques vary among communities.

Communities have a fission-fusion structure: members split into flexible parties and reunite. Males usually stay in their birth community; females may transfer. Grooming, calls, gestures and alliances maintain ties. Tool practices learned socially differ locally: neighbouring groups at Gombe, Tanzania, make different tools for termite fishing.

After about 7½ to 8½ months, a female usually gives birth to one infant. It clings to her and remains dependent for years; nursing often lasts three to four years, followed by continued travel and learning with its mother. This long care period spaces births, though timing varies.

Eating fruit and travelling through forests can disperse seeds; hunting affects prey, including red colobus at Gombe. These effects depend on local foods, prey and habitat. Tools also give access to insects and other hard-to-reach resources.

The IUCN Red List’s 2016 global assessment classified the species as Endangered, citing decline from hunting, habitat loss and degradation, and disease. This is the date of that assessment, not a new population count.

Common carp
Cyprinus carpio

The common carp is a large freshwater fish native to the Black, Caspian and Aral Sea drainages. People have cultured it for food for centuries and transported it widely, creating a sharp distinction between native wild river populations and abundant farmed or introduced fish.

Its deep, slightly compressed body carries large scales and a long-based dorsal fin with a strong spine at the front; the spine’s rear edge bears small serrations. Two pairs of barbels beside the protrusible mouth, which can extend forward, identify it; the upper-lip pair is shorter. Wild fish are usually brownish green above and golden below, while colour and scale coverage vary among cultured strains. Adults commonly measure about 30–60 centimetres and weigh roughly 0.5–4 kilograms. Exceptional fish exceed a metre and 20 kilograms.

Wild carp favor the middle and lower reaches of rivers, floodplains, oxbow lakes and shallow lakes or reservoirs, often over soft bottoms with aquatic vegetation. They feed mainly near the bottom but search through middle and upper water layers as well. Flooded margins are especially important when rising water connects the river to spawning and nursery grounds; dams and channel changes can remove or mistime that access.

A carp pushes its soft, protrusible mouth into sediment and selects edible particles from mud, plant fragments and other debris. Sensitive barbels and taste-rich mouth surfaces help it sort food; modified throat bones bear stout pharyngeal teeth that crush and grind seeds, insect larvae, worms, molluscs and other small prey against a hard chewing pad. It has no true stomach: enzymes digest food along the intestine, where amino acids are absorbed, especially in its front section.

Common carp may feed alone or gather in shifting social groups. At Kleiner Döllnsee, a lake in northern Brandenburg, telemetry of stocked, hatchery-born and pond-reared carp found stronger daytime grouping in winter and smaller, longer-lasting groups in summer. The same individuals met repeatedly, consistent with social memory lasting up to about two weeks; the researchers suggested this could help fish locate patchy food, though they did not identify a communication signal.

In temperate Europe, spawning starts near 17–18 °C, with local variation. In shallow, plant-rich water, females scatter eggs among aquatic plants, where males fertilize them externally. Water makes the egg coat sticky, so eggs adhere to vegetation. Wild females can spawn fractionally, releasing eggs in repeated bouts rather than depositing the full clutch at once; this pattern was documented in the lower River Murray, Australia. At 20–23 °C, embryos develop and hatch in about three days; newly hatched larvae cling to the substrate, then swim horizontally and begin feeding on microscopic aquatic animals called rotifers roughly three days later.

By stirring sediment while feeding, carp release suspended particles and nutrients into the water and can uproot submerged plants. Experiments with juvenile carp found reduced abundance of a submerged pondweed, while a floating-leaved plant increased; turbidity and light availability help determine which species respond. Carp also eat invertebrates, including snails and zooplankton, so they can affect plant growth indirectly through food-web links. Their ecological effects are strongest in some introduced or densely stocked waters and vary with fish size, abundance, habitat and season.

The 2008 IUCN global assessment classified the common carp as Vulnerable. The IUCN Red List update published in 2024 now lists it as Least Concern. The IUCN indicates that this category change does not reflect a genuine improvement in the species’ condition; it therefore does not document a recovery of wild stocks. The 2008 account described native populations in the Black, Caspian and Aral basins as declining, linking the trend to river regulation that disrupts floodplain spawning and hybridization with introduced cultured stocks and related carp.

Common Coot
Fulica atra

The Common Coot is a waterbird of the rail family, widespread across Europe, Africa, Asia and Australasia. Its dark body, bright white bill and frontal shield stand out on lakes, while its unusual toes help it swim, dive and walk on wet ground. Adults measure about 36–38 cm; British ringing samples averaged 880 g, with males heavier than females. The name Eurasian Coot distinguishes it from the separate American Coot, Fulica americana.

The adult is slate-black, with a white bill rising into a smooth white shield on the forehead. This distinguishes it from the smaller Eurasian Moorhen, whose bill and shield are red, and from the American Coot, a separate species. The adult’s red iris is another field mark. Young coots are dark and downy, with a bare orange-red head and pale bill; the adult black-and-white plumage develops gradually.

It prefers still lakes and ponds with open water. It also uses sheltered, sometimes brackish, coastal waters. Shallows let birds reach submerged plants or dive to the bottom. In Britain and Ireland, resident birds are joined in winter by arrivals from farther east; elsewhere, movements vary with weather and freezing.

Aquatic plants are its main food: coots take pondweeds, algae, seeds and shoots. They dive to forage among submerged plants. Their lobed toes propel them underwater. The diet is omnivorous rather than exclusively plant-based: snails, insect larvae and other small invertebrates are also eaten, including as food for chicks.

Each separate toe has its own flexible skin lobe. Thus, unlike a duck, it has no continuous web joining the toes. Take-off is laborious, with a noisy run across the water. Breeding pairs defend territories, rushing at intruders with wings spread. Their calls vary with social context. A study of breeding birds distinguished four call types, with structure changing according to behavior and individual identity. In winter, coots gather in flocks.

A pair builds a platform nest of aquatic stems among reeds or other cover; it may float, anchored to vegetation. Both sexes build, incubate and care for the brood. In Britain, a usual clutch is five to seven eggs, incubated for 21–24 days. Downy chicks swim soon after hatching, but still rely on parents for warmth, protection and food. They fledge at about 55–60 days and may stay with their parents while learning to forage.

Coots feed on aquatic plants and invertebrates, so their foraging connects submerged vegetation and small animal prey in wetland food webs. Otters can provoke alarm calls and a sudden rush away. Reeds and nest platforms shelter chicks; open water helps adults detect danger. Winter flocks gather on productive lakes, where food and resting sites are shared among many birds.

The global Red List assessment dated 14 August 2019 classified the species as Least Concern, with an increasing trend. BirdLife’s 2021 European assessment classified Europe’s population as Near Threatened and decreasing. In Britain, it remains Green-listed, although winter numbers have recently fallen and breeding numbers have declined in some areas. Some Irish breeding-range losses may be linked to wetland drainage.

Common crane
Grus grus

The common crane, also called the Eurasian crane, is a tall, migratory wetland bird: Grus grus links northern breeding grounds with southern wintering areas. It ranges across northern Eurasia, from western Europe to Siberia, and different populations winter in Iberia, Africa, the Middle East or Asia.

Adults are about 115 centimetres tall, weigh around 5.5 kilograms and span roughly 210 centimetres; males average slightly larger and heavier than females. Slate-grey plumage, long dark legs and a long neck create a tall silhouette. The adult has a bare red crown, black forehead and throat, and a white stripe behind the eye. Long wing feathers drape over the short tail like a false train; juveniles have a greyer body and cinnamon-brown head.

Breeding pairs choose quiet, shallow wetlands: bogs, marshes, reedbeds and pools, often with dense shore vegetation. The nest sits in or close to shallow water, which helps conceal it; in winter cranes also use flooded ground, meadows and cultivated fields, returning to communal wetland roosts.

The crane is omnivorous and changes its menu with season and place. It probes soil and shallow water for roots, tubers, seeds and grain, but also eats insects, snails, worms, amphibians, reptiles and small mammals; animal foods become especially important while feeding chicks.

Its loud, trumpeting calls keep birds in contact over open wetlands and warn of danger. Paired cranes answer in a coordinated unison call that reinforces their bond; spring courtship also includes bows, leaps and wing displays. Outside breeding, family groups join larger, shifting flocks that feed by day and gather at traditional roosts at night.

Pairs maintain long-lasting bonds and defend a nesting territory. The female usually lays two eggs in a mound of stems and leaves; both parents incubate them for about 30 days, chiefly the female. Downy chicks leave the nest soon after hatching, walk with their parents and learn to forage; they fledge at about 65–70 days, remain with the family through their first winter, and usually breed successfully at around four years.

Seasonal journeys depend on a chain of wetlands where cranes can nest, rest and roost, while nearby fields provide food. Eggs and small chicks are vulnerable to crows and ravens; foxes and eagles can take older young, and adults defend nests vigorously against ground predators.

The global population is large and the species is assessed as Least Concern, yet local populations have disappeared or declined. Wetland loss, agricultural change and hunting in some regions remain threats, and wintering and migration sites matter as much as breeding marshes. Britain lost its breeding cranes after centuries of wetland drainage; birds returned to Norfolk in 1979, and a WWT–RSPB–Pensthorpe project released 93 young in Somerset between 2010 and 2014, helping rebuild a small regional population.

Common frog
Rana temporaria

The common frog is widespread across Europe and divides its life between water and land. Its cycle links ponds, where eggs and larvae develop, with damp terrestrial places where adults feed and shelter. Adults exchange gases through both their lungs and moist skin; this allows some gas exchange underwater, while powerful hind limbs propel jumps and swimming.

Adults are compact frogs with smooth, damp skin and a dark patch behind the eye covering the eardrum. Their hind legs are moderately long and robust, unlike the agile frog Rana dalmatina, whose legs are very long and slender; exceptions occur, so use several traits together. Colour and markings vary widely, from brown and olive to grey, reddish, yellowish or greenish; colour alone is not enough for identification. In Britain, reported adult lengths reach about 9 cm in males and 13 cm in females, which are generally larger; these are upper figures, not typical sizes everywhere. Where similar brown frogs co-occur, combine several cues, including the eye patch, leg pattern, call and local range, rather than relying on one universal mark.

Across its range, the species uses cool or damp landscapes, from woodland edges, grassland and moor to gardens and farmland. Adults may travel away from water after breeding, so a pond is only one part of their habitat: nearby cover and moist feeding grounds matter too. It breeds in shallow freshwater, including small ponds, lake margins, ditches and sometimes temporary puddles; local populations use the sites available in their landscape.

After metamorphosis, the frog hunts small invertebrates, including insects, slugs, snails and earthworms. It seizes suitable prey with its mouth and sticky tongue, then swallows it; prey size is limited by its mouth. Aquatic tadpoles feed differently: they scrape or gather algae and organic material from surfaces and pond sediment, with animal matter also recorded in some diets. Their feeding links fine detritus and plant growth to larger animals.

The common frog is ectothermic: body temperature and metabolic pace depend strongly on surrounding conditions. It often forages at night or in damp weather, when its skin is less exposed to drying, and retreats beneath vegetation, stones or other cover. In cold seasons, activity and feeding fall and frogs overwinter in sheltered terrestrial sites or in water; refuges vary locally, and this species does not show the extreme freeze tolerance of some other frogs. At breeding ponds, males give a soft, repeated croak to attract mates and compete with nearby males.

Breeding dates shift with spring temperatures and local weather rather than following one universal calendar. In Britain, spawning can start in the southwest in January and is often seen from February onward elsewhere; these are regional examples. Males clasp females in amplexus; as the female releases eggs into water, the male releases sperm over them, so fertilisation is external. Each egg has its own gelatinous covering, and many eggs are laid together as a jelly mass floating just below the water surface. In British ponds, eggs hatch in about three weeks. Tadpoles then breathe underwater with gills. During metamorphosis, lungs develop and take part in air breathing as the gills regress; hind legs appear before forelegs, and the tail is gradually resorbed before froglets leave the water.

Adult frogs and froglets are prey for herons, foxes, otters, snakes and other predators, while their aquatic eggs and tadpoles face fish, newts and insect larvae. The frog thus links terrestrial and pond food webs as both predator and prey.

The global IUCN assessment dates to 14 December 2008 and was published in 2009. It classified Rana temporaria as Least Concern with a stable trend, but the Red List record says this assessment needs updating; this historic result does not establish current status. Regional pressures include loss or degradation of breeding ponds and disease. In Britain, Natural England says garden ponds have partly offset the loss of traditional farm ponds. Protecting pond networks and nearby cover supports the full life cycle.

Common fruit fly
Drosophila melanogaster

Despite its common name, Drosophila melanogaster is a vinegar fly in the family Drosophilidae, not a tephritid true fruit fly. Its short generations and well-studied genetics made it a landmark model for studying animal heredity and development.

Adults are about 3 millimetres long, with females slightly larger than males. The thorax bears six legs and clear forewings; small knob-shaped halteres, the altered hindwings, help stabilize flight. Wild-type flies have reddish eyes and a yellow-brown body with dark abdominal bands; the male’s abdomen is darker toward the rear.
Originally African, it now occurs worldwide. It gathers where fruit, plant juices and other foods ferment, from orchards and markets to kitchens and restaurants.
Larvae and adults exploit fermenting fruit together with its yeasts, bacteria and other microbes; the patch supplies microbial food as well as a suitable place for young flies to develop.

Adults often gather around fermenting food. During courtship, a male follows and taps a female, vibrates one wing to sing, then licks her before attempting to mate; she may reject him. The exchange combines sound, touch and chemical cues.

After mating, the female stores sperm and lays successive fertilized eggs on suitable decaying food; she can lay roughly 400 eggs over time. At about 25 °C in standard laboratory conditions, eggs hatch in roughly a day; larvae feed and moult twice through three stages, then pupate before adults emerge. This egg-to-adult cycle takes about ten days under those laboratory conditions. Females may become receptive to mating within about 8–12 hours of emergence, depending on temperature.

By feeding and breeding in decomposing fruit, flies ingest microbes and return them to the substrate in their droppings, helping maintain a shared fruit–microbe–fly community and carrying microbes between temporary patches of decay. Yeasts and bacteria do not just share the patch: they shape its food value and microbial conditions for the next brood.
The species is globally widespread and commonly gathers in homes, restaurants and other places where food is served, where people often regard it as a nuisance.

Common moorhen
Gallinula chloropus

The common moorhen is a medium-sized member of the rail family, widespread in Europe, Africa and Asia. It lives at the boundary between land and fresh water, using both vegetated shores and the water surface. The similar American common gallinule, Gallinula galeata, is a separate species; American records published under the old combined name do not describe its present range.

Adults are about 32–35 centimetres long, weigh roughly 250–400 grams and have a 50–55 centimetre wingspan. The back and wings are dark brown, contrasting with bluish-black underparts; white streaks mark the flanks. The red bill ends in a yellow tip, and the frontal shield is red. Greenish legs and white patches beneath the tail are conspicuous when the bird walks or flicks its tail. A coot instead has a white bill and forehead.

Vegetated lake margins, ponds, marshes and rivers provide feeding places and shelter. The moorhen readily occupies park ponds and other small urban wetlands, as well as rural waters. Dense waterside plants let it withdraw from danger, although it also ventures into open spaces. Its nest may rest among floating plants, on a small island or in a tree above the water.

It is an omnivore, eating water plants, seeds, fruit and grasses as well as insects, snails, worms and small fish. Food is gathered both in water and on land: it picks items from the surface, dips its head to reach submerged food, or grazes and searches vegetation along the shore. This varied feeding strategy allows it to exploit the foods available locally rather than depend on a single kind of prey.

During spring courtship, a male approaches a female with its bill dipped in the water; the partners may then nibble at each other’s feathers. Both build and fiercely defend the nest. When disturbed, a moorhen usually runs into nearby cover instead of immediately flying away. If it does fly locally, the flight is often short and laboured. Outside breeding, winter feeding groups can form, while northern populations move away from severe cold.

British nesting records indicate usually five to seven eggs, incubated by both parents for about 20–22 days, and commonly two broods in a season. The chicks hatch covered in down and already mobile. Mobility does not mean immediate independence: adults continue to feed them, and older siblings sometimes help. Flight develops at roughly eight weeks, much later than the chicks’ first movements around the nest.

Family relationships can extend beyond a single brood. Some independent young from the first brood remain on their natal territory and feed younger siblings from a second brood. In a three-year study, adults with juvenile helpers reduced their own feeding effort, while the total feeding rate of the family remained similar. Such cooperation changes how care is shared between parents and offspring, rather than simply multiplying every chick’s food supply.

The species is listed globally as Least Concern, but local trends need separate attention. In the United Kingdom it entered the Amber list of conservation concern in the 2021 assessment. BTO’s winter series shows a 25 percent decrease between 1998 and 2023; these counts include continental visitors as well as residents. Loss of wetlands can isolate local populations and increase their vulnerability, despite the species’ ability to use modified and urban environments.

Common nightingale

The common nightingale is a small, ground-foraging Old World flycatcher whose celebrated song carries through European scrub in spring. It breeds across Europe and parts of western and central Asia, then crosses the Sahara to winter in sub-Saharan Africa.

Adults are about 15–16.5 cm long, and the sexes look alike in plumage. Brown upperparts, a reddish tail, pale unspotted underparts, a fine bill and relatively long legs give this secretive bird a plain, upright appearance; juveniles are spotted. British ringing samples put adult mass around 18–24 g.

Breeding birds favour dense scrub and young woodland with low, leafy cover and patches of bare soil beneath. They place their nest on or close to the ground, concealed among leaves and stems; this structure provides cover and nearby foraging ground.

It takes insects and other small invertebrates, especially beetles and ants, searching through leaf litter and low vegetation with short hops and pauses. In late summer and autumn, berries and other fruits supplement this animal prey.

Males produce loud, varied whistles, trills and bubbling phrases to attract females and advertise or defend a breeding territory. Night song is especially associated with unpaired males seeking mates; after pairing, males usually stop singing regularly at night, so not every individual sings nocturnally all season.

The female builds a low cup of dead leaves and grasses, lined with finer plant material, feathers or hair, and usually lays four or five eggs. She incubates them for about 14 days; downy, helpless chicks are fed in the nest and normally fledge at 11–13 days. Leaving the nest is not independence: young remain near cover while learning to forage and continue to rely on adults afterward.
Ground-foraging nightingales take invertebrates, while raptors and mammals prey on them; low dense scrub gives cover to nests and newly fledged young.

The global IUCN assessment published in 2017, based on a 2016 assessment, classified the species as Least Concern. In Britain, BTO describes the localized breeding population as declining; deer browsing and scrub loss or maturation reduce suitable low cover, and winter-ground changes may also affect returning birds.

Common octopus
Octopus vulgaris

The Common Octopus is a soft-bodied coastal cephalopod, adapted to reefs and seabed shelters. Octopus vulgaris sensu stricto is documented in the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic. Earlier worldwide records often treated related lineages as one species. The American Atlantic lineage is recognized as O. americanus. The East Asian common octopus is O. sinensis. Its short life links planktonic young to solitary, bottom-living adults.

Its rounded mantle houses the organs; the head bears large eyes and a beak amid eight arms. These are arms, not tentacles: each carries two rows of suckers for gripping, tasting and handling food or shelter. Typical mantle length is 10–20 cm and mass 1–3 kg; the reported maximum is about 10 kg, with males tending to grow larger. Ten kilograms is exceptional; skin colour ranges from grey to yellow or reddish brown and its texture can rise into bumps.

Adults occupy coastal seabeds, often rocky or sandy, mostly within about 100 m. A crevice or rock cavity provides a den for shelter and retreat after foraging. They are generally solitary, and den use varies with local prey and shelter.

It hunts bottom-living prey, chiefly crabs and other crustaceans, bivalves and snails. Shells and prey remains near dens reveal part of the diet, but currents and carried-away prey make such middens incomplete evidence. The arms and suckers hold prey while the beak bites. Octopuses drill holes into shells to reach the soft tissue inside. The toothed salivary papilla acts as an accessory radula during drilling. Salivary enzymes help process prey, and nutrients are absorbed through the digestive gland.

An arm is a muscular hydrostat: interwoven lengthwise, transverse and oblique muscles bend, shorten, extend and twist it without rigid bones. Arm nerve networks coordinate local movement within a connected nervous system; the popular phrase “nine brains” oversimplifies this arrangement. Suckers attach, explore and sense surfaces. Chromatophores are pigment sacs expanded by radial muscle contraction; iridophores reflect light, while muscular papillae change skin relief. In a captive spatial-reversal study, some individuals learned to change a rewarded choice when feedback was available, evidence of flexible learning in that specific laboratory task.

Males transfer sperm packets with a specialized right third arm, the hectocotylus. A female attaches 100,000–500,000 eggs, each about 2 mm long, in strings inside a sheltered den. She cleans and ventilates the clutch with water jets and generally stops feeding while brooding. The species reproduces once: females die after hatching, and males undergo terminal decline after mating. In Senegal, eggs hatched in 15–42 days at 27 degrees Celsius but took 80–87 days at 17 degrees Celsius. Hatchlings are planktonic paralarvae, not miniature benthic adults; a regional rearing study recorded settlement after about 40–60 days at 18–22 degrees Celsius. These timings vary with region and water temperature.

The life cycle spans two food webs: paralarvae eat zooplankton, while adults prey on seabed invertebrates. Currents disperse young, and temperature and circulation affect development and juvenile supply to coasts. Adults also feed larger fish and marine mammals. The octopus therefore links plankton, benthic prey and coastal predators.

The species is commercially exploited. Its short life cycle makes annual abundance sensitive to recruitment success. A 2008 northwest African stock assessment, published by FAO in 2011, classed the Dakhla, Cap Blanc and Senegal–Gambia stocks as overexploited and recommended lower fishing effort; this is a dated regional finding. The European Commission lists a 750 g minimum conservation reference size for relevant fisheries, a management rule rather than a guarantee of population security.

Common pheasant
Phasianus colchicus
The common pheasant is a large ground-dwelling bird native to temperate Asia, introduced elsewhere by people.

Adults have a compact body, strong legs and a long tapering tail; males are usually larger, often 75–90 cm long including the tail. The male is vividly coloured with a red face, green head and copper body; females are smaller and mottled brown, and the white neck ring is not universal.

Its native range reaches from the Caucasus and western Asia through China, across open woodland, scrub and grassland with nearby dense cover. Introductions spread it through Europe and North America, where self-sustaining wild populations coexist with farmed birds and seasonal releases. It also uses field margins, hedges and grassy ditches for shelter beside feeding areas.

It scratches the ground for seeds, grains, roots and fallen fruit, adding leaves and buds; in spring and summer it takes more insects and other invertebrates. Newly hatched chicks rely especially on animal prey before their diet shifts toward more plant food over the following weeks.

Breeding males announce and defend territories with loud calls, wing-drumming and spread-tail displays; one male may mate with several inconspicuous females. The species usually walks or runs, but when startled it launches almost vertically with rattling wingbeats, then flies a short distance to cover. Outside breeding, females may gather in flocks, with larger groups in winter than in summer.

The female lays about 7–15 eggs in a shallow ground nest and alone incubates them for roughly 23–28 days; downy chicks leave soon after hatching, feed themselves, follow her, and can make short flights at about two weeks.

Pheasants forage along field margins, while foxes and other predators take eggs and chicks. Introduced birds can compete with native gamebirds for food and nesting space, so local effects vary with habitat and release density.

The global IUCN assessment published in 2016 classified it as Least Concern but reported a decreasing trend. That assessment estimated 160–220 million mature birds worldwide, despite declines in parts of its range.

Common Ringed Plover
Charadrius hiaticula

The common ringed plover is a small, dumpy wader that nests in the open on beaches. Its eggs and chicks are so well camouflaged that the birds are easily disturbed, and people on beaches are a major cause of its decline in Britain.

The upperparts are greyish-brown and the underparts white, with a white collar and forehead. In summer it has a black breast band and a black “bandit” mask across the eyes, which fade to brown in winter. The bill is blunt, orange with a black tip, and the legs are bright orange. Adults weigh about 54–82 g.

It breeds mainly on the coast, especially on sandy and shingle beaches, and in the Uists on machair. Inland it also uses gravel pits, river margins, lochsides and wet meadows. In the UK, resident birds stay all year and migrants from the north pass through.

It feeds on coastal and terrestrial invertebrates such as beetles, marine worms, amphipods, isopods, molluscs and spiders. It hunts by sight, running, stopping and pecking, and sometimes trembles a foot on the sand to draw prey out.

Males defend territories with tail-fanning, sparring and chases, and advertise them with slow “butterfly” flights. A male makes a shallow scrape in the shingle and shows it to the female in a “scrape ceremony”. Adults feign a broken wing to lure predators away, and the chicks crouch and hide.

In Britain the average first clutch date is about 14 May, and pairs typically raise two broods, occasionally three. A clutch is usually four eggs, incubated by both sexes for 23–25 days. The downy chicks fledge after about 23–25 days. Breeding typically starts at one year old.

The speckled eggs blend into sand and shingle, but they are easily trampled. Disturbance on beaches reduces nesting success, and introduced hedgehogs eat eggs in the Western Isles. One estimate suggests that keeping people off beaches could raise the population by about 85%.

The IUCN global category is Least Concern, but the species is Red-listed in the UK. The UK breeding population was 5,450 pairs in 2007, after a fall of about 37% between 1984 and 2007, with the largest declines inland. A bird that reaches breeding age lives about five years; the oldest ringed bird reached almost 22.

Common Sandpiper
Actitis hypoleucos

The common sandpiper is a small wader that nests beside fast-flowing water and migrates to Africa and beyond for the winter. It is easily recognised by its constant bobbing and its low flight over the water.

In Britain adults weigh about 58 g, with a wing near 112 mm; females are slightly bigger than males. The upperparts are brown, with a sharply defined white breast, and the tail is relatively long. It bobs its head and tail when walking, and flies low with stiff, bowed wings, flicking them.

In Britain it breeds mainly along upland rivers and lochs, nesting in vegetation beside the water. Across its wider range it also uses sandy coasts and riverbanks, and in winter it visits ponds, rivers, estuaries and mangroves.
It eats mainly small invertebrates such as insects, worms, spiders and crustaceans, picked up as it runs along the shoreline. It occasionally takes small amphibians or fish.

Pairs hold long, narrow territories along the water and defend them with noisy display flights. Males defend territory and mate with threat displays. It is a long-distance migrant: tracked Scottish birds wintered mainly on the coast of Guinea-Bissau.

In Britain a clutch is typically four eggs, incubated for 21–22 days by both parents. The downy chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and feed themselves, fledging at about 19 days. Birds first breed at about two years old.

The common sandpiper preys on small invertebrates along waterways and is itself eaten by animals such as foxes, weasels and gulls. Its mottled brown back provides camouflage on stony and muddy shores, and it often carries blood parasites.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide. In the UK it is Amber-listed, with about 13,000 breeding pairs in 2016. The oldest ringed bird reached 15 years, though a typical breeding-age adult lives about 8.

Common swift
Apus apus

The common swift is a bird built around open air: it catches food, drinks, gathers nest material and often rests while flying. Its brief breeding season is the exception, when a pair returns to a cavity to raise its young. The species usually raises one brood in a year, then leaves its European breeding grounds for Africa as summer ends.

In British adults, the mean wing length is about 175 mm and mean body mass is 39.5 g. Their sooty-brown plumage, pale throat, long swept-back wings and short forked tail form a dark, curved silhouette overhead; the small throat patch is easily missed as they speed past.

It breeds across much of Europe and Asia, nesting in enclosed spaces such as roof gaps, eaves, old walls, cliffs and tree hollows. In Britain and Ireland, swifts nest almost entirely in buildings, where roof cavities can support colonies even in busy towns. Outside the breeding season, tracked birds range across sub-Saharan Africa, with winter destinations differing among European populations.

The swift takes flying insects and spiders, from aphids and flies to beetles and small wasps, sweeping them from the air with its wide gape. Adults accumulate many tiny prey in a saliva-bound throat pouch, then regurgitate the compact food bolus to their chicks; its contents change with the insects available. Both adults forage in the air and bring this concentrated meal back to the nest, where several small prey items arrive together rather than one at a time.

Long, narrow, sickle-shaped wings and short feathered feet suit rapid, agile flight and gliding, while making take-off from level ground difficult. Swifts call with piercing screams as they wheel in social groups near nest sites. Tracking showed that during the ten-month non-breeding period, tagged birds spent over 99% of their time airborne; this does not describe the breeding season. Most tracked birds nevertheless showed occasional periods without flight.

A pair lays a usual clutch of two or three eggs in a shallow cup of feathers and plant fibres glued with saliva inside a cavity. Both parents incubate for about 18–24 days and feed the naked, helpless hatchlings. Young normally leave the nest after roughly 37–56 days, with timing affected by conditions; they then fly independently. The species generally rears a single brood during its short stay on the breeding grounds.

By feeding on airborne arthropods, swifts are tied to weather: cold or prolonged rain can make prey harder to find and adults less able to forage, leaving nestlings short of food. Researchers have confirmed occasional nocturnal torpor in families resting in nests during cold breeding-season nights; torpor is a temporary, controlled reduction in metabolism, not a routine state for every bird. In a monitored Italian colony, nestling survival also varied with hatching order and brood conditions, showing how a spell of poor feeding can affect the youngest chicks.

BTO monitoring shows that British breeding numbers fell by 70% between 1995 and 2024. Building renovations close roof gaps and remove nest sites; this loss contributed to the swift’s addition to the UK red list in 2021.

Brown Shrimp
Crangon crangon

The brown shrimp, or common shrimp, is a small crustacean of European shallow coasts that buries itself in sand and is fished commercially. It is one of the most abundant animals of sandy bays and estuaries, and a key food for fish and wading birds.

The body is long, thin and mottled brown, slightly flattened from top to bottom, and its colour matches the sediment. The rostrum is short and blunt, the first walking leg is subchelate (a small hook-like claw), and the telson has two pairs of lateral spines. Females grow larger than males, with a reported maximum of about 8.5–9.5 cm, rarely reached.

It lives on sandy and muddy bottoms from the intertidal zone to about 150 m deep, in open coast, estuaries, lagoons and bays, and prefers sediment with grains of 125–710 µm. Its range runs along European coasts from the White Sea to Morocco, and into the Mediterranean and Black Seas. It tolerates a very wide range of salinity.

It is an omnivorous predator and scavenger that forages mostly at night. It eats polychaete worms, small fish, molluscs, small crustaceans and green seaweeds such as sea lettuce. Newly settled juveniles rely on the annual bloom of copepods.

The shrimp buries itself in 9–10 seconds by beating its abdominal limbs and sweeping sand over its back, leaving only the eyes and antennae out, to hide from predators and ambush prey. It can swim, crawl or walk. Adults move offshore from November to March to avoid low-salinity water, and young shrimps use inshore nurseries for a few weeks.

Breeding is spread over much of the year, with summer eggs (up to 4,500 per female) and larger winter eggs (up to 2,800) produced from October–November; females carry them for 4 to 13 weeks depending on temperature. Planktonic larvae live 1 to 6 months, and juveniles settle from May to July. Maturity comes at 35–50 mm, and whether the species changes sex is debated.

Gulls, terns, redshanks, cod relatives, flatfish, gurnards and young bass eat brown shrimps, which can reach about 60 per square metre in summer peaks. Most individuals are in their first year class; the maximum age reported is about 3 years in one source and up to 5 in females in another. Black spot shell disease affects between 13% and 87% of shrimps in British sites.

No conservation category was found in the sources read. European landings rose from about 5,000 t in 1950 to nearly 29,000 t in 1997, taken mainly by beam trawl; about half of a catch is undersized. High fecundity and fast turnover let populations recover quickly.

Corn Crake
Crex crex

The corn crake is a small, brown and secretive bird of the rail family. Unlike its relatives the moorhen and the coot, it lives on dry land, hidden in tall grass, so it is far more often heard than seen.

A medium-sized rail, 27–30 cm long, weighing about 150 g (151 g on average in Britain). The back is brown-black streaked with buff, the wings show chestnut patches, the face, neck and breast are blue-grey, and the flanks are barred chestnut and white. The bill is flesh-coloured and the legs pale grey.
On its breeding grounds it favours meadows: cool, moist hayfields and traditional grassland that is cut late and lightly fertilised. In winter it lives in dry grassland and savanna in Africa.
It eats mainly invertebrates such as earthworms, slugs, snails, beetles and grasshoppers. It also takes small frogs and mammals, grass seeds and cereal grain.
The male gives a loud, rasping advertising call, a repeated “krek krek” that carries up to about 1.5 km. The species migrates at night between Europe and Africa, arriving in Britain from April.

The nest is a scrape on the ground lined with grass. A clutch is typically 8–12 eggs (range 6–14), incubated by the female alone for 16–19 days. The downy chicks leave the nest within a day or two and fledge after 34–38 days; one or two broods are raised per season. Breeding typically starts at one year of age.

Cats, foxes, weasels, rats and birds such as buzzards and crows prey on corn crakes and their chicks. The greatest danger comes from early mechanical mowing, which destroys nests and kills chicks hidden in the grass.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern; it was Near Threatened until 2010. In Europe it numbers an estimated 1.3–2.0 million breeding pairs, about three-quarters of them in Russia. In the UK it is Red-listed: about 1,100 calling males bred in 2013–17, and 904 were counted in 2019. Typical life expectancy is only about two years.
